name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Sandbox classroom preps kids for careers as heavy equipment operators
description: St. Paul Public Schools has officially opened a what the district calls a sandbox classroom, but it’s not for little kids. Instead, it’s part of the district’s new program that trains high school seniors to operate heavy equipment on the path to high-paying jobs in construction. Kyle Ring is one of the students who prefers […]
text:
Instructor Dusty Thune sets up a surveyor's laser level to check Alicia Xiong's work as she learns how to grade land on the first "sandbox" classroom in the Twin Cities, opened via a partnership between Saint Paul Public Schools, IUOE Local 49, Minnesota Virtual Academy and the St. Paul Port Authority Tuesday, May 19, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)St. Paul Public Schools has officially opened a what the district calls a sandbox classroom, but it’s not for little kids. Instead, it’s part of the district’s new program that trains high school seniors to operate heavy equipment on the path to high-paying jobs in construction.
Kyle Ring is one of the students who prefers this hands-on learning. He and 14 other high school seniors in St. Paul Public Schools have been enrolled in the program since September, but they have only been in the sandbox since it opened May 11. Still, he and the program’s teacher, Dusty Thune, say the ability to work with actual equipment — instead of just a computer simulation — has been great for the students.
“Getting the hands-on experience has been everything,” Thune said. “You have to have a lot of seat hours in order to start understanding where you are in space with these big machines.”
“Being on the simulators, yes, it’s good for us, but it doesn’t have the same feel because we are sitting moving in the machine,” Ring said. 
Since the sandbox classroom opened, the students have been able to use an excavator and bulldozer to practice skills like building a graded surface.
The International Union of Operating Engineers Local 49, which represents members across Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota, approached the district more than a year ago about adding a career and technical education program. The program, whose launch last year was supported by a broad coalition of public and private sector partners, allows the district’s high school seniors to enroll in four courses. Students earn credit toward their high school diploma, apprenticeship hours with the union and even college credit, if they want to pursue higher ed.
The union gets to nurture future members; employers get subsidized training; and the school district fulfills its educational mission — everyone wins. 
The union started a statewide, online career and tech program seven years ago, through Minnesota Virtual Academy, an online charter school. This year over 350 students across the state were enrolled in that program. 
Although many students thrive in the program’s online format, others said they wanted a more traditional experience. Partnering with local school districts to build sandbox classrooms is one way Local 49 is addressing student demand for hands-on learning.
In addition to the work in the sandbox, the program includes field trips to places like the Minnesota Department of Transportation to learn about the science of building materials, and the airport and Ramsey and Washington counties to learn about snow removal. For many students, getting out of a traditional classroom setting can help keep them engaged in school.
Peter Flower learns how to grade land on the first “sandbox” classroom in the Twin Cities, opened via a partnership between Saint Paul Public Schools, IUOE Local 49, Minnesota Virtual Academy and the St. Paul Port Authority Tuesday, May 19, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Thune says that in addition to the field trips, the small class sizes foster a close-knit community, which also keeps them engaged.
“And not just in our class. They’re asking for help with their other studies, trying to get caught up on tests or understanding concepts that they weren’t quite getting in class. They’re able to ask their peers; they’re able to ask us teachers. And we’re able to give a little bit more help than would normally be given,” Thune said.
Jenny Winkelaar, director of workforce and community development for Local 49, said students in the program have gained confidence since the beginning of the year. Last fall, Ames Construction hosted a heavy equipment rodeo, where operators can show off their skills; several St. Paul students attended. She said most were shy, hesitant to participate and didn’t want to make eye contact. But at the ribbon cutting for the sandbox classroom, she said the students were all excited to get into the equipment and show off their skills.
“It went from taking a step backward and avoiding eye contact to calling dibs on the excavator. It is really cool to watch them evolve,” Winkelaar said.
With school districts struggling to keep up with rising costs, outside groups were critical to bringing the sandbox to fruition.
The St. Paul Port Authority is leasing the land for the classroom to the school district for $1 per year. Local 49 has covered the cost of a teacher and paraprofessional for this school year and next. And 12 private sector firms donated all the materials, labor and project management to build the sandbox.
“It took so many diverse stakeholders coming together and really just keeping the goal at the forefront of wanting to create this opportunity for students within the St. Paul Public Schools,” Winkelaar said.
Operating engineers must complete about 6,000 hours of training as an apprentice before they can work as a journeyman. Most of those hours are paid, on the job, earning $27-37 per hour plus benefits. The wages are significantly higher than some other career and technical education pathways, according to Thune.
Becoming an apprentice requires an employer sponsor. For students in the pathway program, Local 49 is helping them connect with employers. So far, they have arranged two in-person meetings for students with both public and private employers. 
The union’s career navigator, Akeethia Lloyd, is also helping students prepare their resumes and connect with potential employers. Lloyd graduated from North High School in Minneapolis. Winkelaar says Lloyd is dedicated to making sure that urban high school students are aware of the career opportunities for heavy equipment operators, and mentoring them through their apprenticeship to help them be successful. 
If they can succeed in programs like this one, there’s work waiting for them: More than 46,000 heavy equipment operator job openings per year are expected during the next decade nationwide, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. 
Kyle Ring and Alicia Xiong learn how to grade land on the first “sandbox” classroom in the Twin Cities, opened via a partnership between Saint Paul Public Schools, IUOE Local 49, Minnesota Virtual Academy and the St. Paul Port Authority Tuesday, May 19, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)
Traditionally, apprentices mostly learned about job opportunities through family or friends. This limited who had access to the industry to people with industry connections. Local 49 is trying to diversify its workforce through career and technical education programs, creating a pipeline into the profession, even if they don’t already know someone in the field.
One barrier for students in St. Paul is that the apprenticeship requires a drivers license. According to Thune, most of his students don’t have access to their own vehicle, and obtaining a drivers license can be challenging for students who live in the city.
Another barrier: Although the courses count toward the general credits they need for high school graduation, they don’t fulfill graduation requirements in specific classes. Winkelaar said that Local 49 is working with the Department of Education to get the pathways math course to count as one of the math classes students need to graduate, for instance.
Thune says most of his 15 students, including Ring, are hoping to go directly to work after they graduate this spring. But two students plan to enroll in post-secondary education in construction. Central Lakes College offers a two-year program in heavy equipment operation and maintenance. The students can transfer their apprenticeship  hours to North Hennepin Community College towards a two-year degree, and to Minnesota State in Moorhead for a four-year degree in construction management. 
“I like the opportunity this class gives us because we not only get to go on field trips and do hands-on things, it offers more opportunities for the future than some classes would,” Ring said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Physician given a warning over ‘inappropriate relationship’ with patient
description: The Iowa Board of Medicine has issued a warning to a physician accused of cultivating an inappropriate relationship with a patient. The board recently charged Raymond M. Tamburro with unprofessional conduct in violation of Iowa Administrative Code 481-655.5 (4). That rule speaks to “sexual conduct” and prohibits “contact, touching or comments of a sexual nat[...]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Medicine)The Iowa Board of Medicine has issued a warning to a physician accused of cultivating an inappropriate relationship with a patient.
The board recently charged Raymond M. Tamburro with unprofessional conduct in violation of Iowa Administrative Code 481-655.5 (4). That rule speaks to “sexual conduct” and prohibits “contact, touching or comments of a sexual nature with a patient.”
According to the board, it received an unspecified number of complaints in 2025 that alleged Tamburro had engaged in “an inappropriate relationship with a patient while in his residency.” The board alleges that Tamburro first saw the patient at a MercyOne clinic in Mason City on June 2, 2025, then saw the patient two more times over the next two weeks.
After the first appointment, the board alleges, Tamburro texted the patient about her test results, and the interaction then “progressed to texting about other issues” and to “meeting with the patient outside of the clinic.”
According to the board, Tamburro was investigated by MercyOne and was fired on Oct. 7, 2025, for engaging in an inappropriate relationship with a patient.
Board records indicate that in order to resolve the disciplinary case without a hearing, Tamburro recently consented to a settlement agreement with the board.
As part of the settlement, Tamburro has agreed to be cited for unprofessional conduct and to accept a warning that engaging in such conduct in the future could result in disciplinary action against his license. The settlement also stipulates that Tamburro must complete an educational course of unspecified duration on professional boundaries and ethics.
Tamburro declined to comment on the matter when contacted Tuesday by the Iowa Capital Dispatch.
State records indicate Tamburro was first issued an Iowa medical resident license on July 3, 2023. Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services records indicate he is currently a licensed physician in that state with no record of any disciplinary action involving his Nebraska license.

name: VTDigger
title: Lily Pierce finds her calling in sign language
description:
What began as a middle school class grew into a passion for language and human connection. As a first-generation student, Lily navigated the college search and financial aid process with determination, finding a path to a career where she will help others communicate and be understood.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lily Pierce finds her calling in sign[...]
text:
The expressive nature of sign language resonates with Lily, who is captivated by its ability to connect people and communicate emotion. “Hearing people don’t always connect that emotion with their words and expressions,” she said. “Learning ASL really changed my perspective and how I see communication.” 
Lily’s outlook was solidified when her American Sign Language (ASL) class took a full-immersion trip to Gallaudet University in Washington D.C., a school uniquely designed to accommodate deaf and hard-of-hearing students. There Lily and her class experienced the power of vocal silence, using only their ASL to communicate. Absorbed in Gallaudet’s friendly and welcoming community, the opportunity stuck with Lily and motivated her to support accessibility for, and awareness of, the deaf community. 
A career in ASL interpretation
Lily has a lot of paths to choose from that will align with her interest in a career in ASL interpretation, including medical and legal interpretation, or education. Right now, she’s leaning toward helping kids, and may pursue a future in education. But first, she needs to pursue her own education in order to get there. 
Lily is seventeen, and soon will graduate from Williamstown High School. She’s headed to Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) in the fall and will be studying ASL there. Her interest in ASL was first kindled in middle school, when she started taking ASL classes. She continued through high school, and this year was even able to take a few Early College classes through Norwich University to get postsecondary experience in ASL. 
Motivated by RIT’s tough but rewarding curriculum, Lily is looking forward to her new school. She visited RIT twice and fell in love with the campus and community, and she says that the college is welcoming, with a good reputation and learning environment.
Figuring out the college application and financial aid process as a first-generation student
As a first-generation college student, Lily found navigating the college search and financial aid process daunting. “My parents didn’t go to college,” she said, “so we really relied on my VSAC counselor, Chelsea Martin, for the whole list of things we had to do and think about.” Chelsea works as an outreach counselor in VSAC’s Talent Search program, which helps modest income, first-generation students explore opportunities after high school. Lily began meeting with Chelsea during her sophomore year at Williamstown. 
Lily and Chelsea brainstormed ideas and plans. Chelsea suggested Early College as a way for Lily to get some college credits and course experience. Junior year, they worked in earnest, meeting monthly and making a list of colleges with strong ASL programs that might fit what Lily was looking for. “Senior year, I needed extra help,” Lily laughed. “I was reaching out to Chelsea all the time and checking in.” 
That help continued through the application process; Lily applied to eight different colleges. Chelsea helped her work through the financial aid paperwork and identified several scholarships from the VSAC Scholarship Booklet for which Lily could apply. Lily is waiting to hear back on a few of her scholarship applications; however, she received a workable financial aid package from RIT and feels comfortable with what she might need to take out in student loans, and her ability to pay them off after graduation. 
A supportive family and a love of learning
Lily’s parents are incredibly supportive, encouraging her to pursue this dream and to apply for the scholarships that will help her get there. “I’ve always kind of known I would go to college,” Lily said. “I knew I would want to keep doing school, stay engaged, and keep learning.” 
That love of learning is something she fosters in younger children as well. She loves working with kids and coaches third and fourth grade girls’ basketball for the local AAU program, in addition to high school commitments, including the athletic leadership committee, basketball, track and field, and yearbook.  
When Lily heads to college in the fall, she knows she’ll stay engaged and motivated in her academics. She’s looking forward to having a little self-determined free time as well, and says she can’t wait for the opportunity to experience something new and different!
The Vermont Student Assistance Corp. was created by the Vermont Legislature in 1965 as a public nonprofit agency. We advocate for Vermont students and their families to ensure that they have the tools they need to achieve their education and training goals. We create opportunities for all Vermont students, but particularly for those—of any age—who believe that the doors to education are closed to them. Growing families save for education with VT529, Vermont’s official 529 savings program. To help Vermonters plan and pay for college or job training, our counselors work with students in nearly every Vermont middle school and high school, and are also available to work with adults. Our grant, scholarship, and workforce development programs create opportunity, help students re-skill or learn new skills, and grow the economy. VSAC’s loan, loan refinance, and loan forgiveness programs provide competitive education financing to students and families. Find us at www.vsac.org or visit Facebook, Instagram, or LinkedIn.

name: Delaware
title: GradBridge headquarters move shows Delaware fintech plan paying off
description: The student lending startup plans 49 high-paying jobs in Newark, reinforcing Delaware’s push to become a national fintech hub. WILMINGTON — Delaware’s long-running effort to build a statewide financial technology economy is beginning to show tangible results, with GradBridge LLC selecting Newark for its headquarters and committing to create 49 full-time jobs[...]
text:
The student lending startup plans 49 high-paying jobs in Newark, reinforcing Delaware’s push to become a national fintech hub.
WILMINGTON — Delaware’s long-running effort to build a statewide financial technology economy is beginning to show tangible results, with GradBridge LLC selecting Newark for its headquarters and committing to create 49 full-time jobs over the next five years.
The Delaware-founded fintech startup and private student lending platform will locate in a 9,321-square-foot space at Iron Hill Corporate Center on Prides Crossing. The decision follows a Mid-Atlantic search that included Philadelphia and reflects the state’s broader strategy to turn its financial services history, legal framework, university research capacity and workforce pipeline into a competitive advantage for high-growth fintech companies.
Long-term fintech strategy takes shape
GradBridge’s move comes as Delaware, the University of Delaware and Delaware Technology Park continue to build out a long-term vision for a FinTech Park and Innovation Hub at UD’s STAR Campus. That plan is designed to make Delaware more than a traditional banking and corporate law center. The goal is to position the state as a national and potentially global hub for fintech innovation, regulation, workforce development and financial equity.
For Delaware economic development officials, the GradBridge announcement offers an early example of that strategy in action: a startup choosing the state not only because of incentives, but because of its access to financial services talent, regulatory expertise and proximity to major institutions such as Barclays, JPMorgan Chase, WSFS and Sallie Mae.
High-wage jobs planned in Newark
The company had four permanent full-time employees in Delaware at the end of 2025. It plans to add jobs in executive leadership, finance, compliance, credit, data analytics and management. All of the new positions are expected to be salaried and benefit-eligible, with nearly all paying more than $110,000 annually.
Gov. Matt Meyer said the expansion supports Delaware’s effort to grow its innovation economy, especially in sectors such as fintech that can bring high-wage jobs and new business activity to the state.
“Delaware is proving once again that it is the best place for high-growth companies to launch, scale and succeed,” Meyer said. “GradBridge’s expansion in Newark brings nearly 50 high-quality jobs to our state and reinforces Delaware’s reputation as a leader in financial innovation. This investment is a win for our workforce, our economy and the future of fintech in Delaware.”
Student lending platform targets near-approval borrowers
GradBridge is a “second-look” private student lending platform designed for borrowers who fall just outside traditional credit standards. The company says more than 1 million near-approval borrowers are declined annually, often leaving students with a funding gap as they work toward completing a degree.
The company focuses on upperclassmen and graduate students who are making academic progress but still need financing to graduate. Its model operates within a sponsor bank framework and an originate-and-sell structure, which the company says allows it to scale while maintaining disciplined risk management and efficient capital use.
GradBridge is backed by Acorn Investment Partners, a portfolio company of funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management L.P. Its operating partners include CampusDoor, Hatch Bank, Nelnet/Firstmark and Gestalt.
Jen O’Donald, chief executive officer of GradBridge, said the company’s Delaware headquarters will support both its student lending mission and its investment in local talent.
“We at GradBridge are passionate about removing financial barriers to higher education, and I am grateful to both the Council on Development Finance and Delaware Prosperity Partnership for supporting that goal,” O’Donald said. “With their support, we will build more than a headquarters, we will create economic opportunity by investing in local talent and bridging the gap to graduation for more students nationwide.”
State support tied to job creation
Delaware Prosperity Partnership logo
The company expects to invest up to $250,000 to update and fit out its Newark office.
Delaware Prosperity Partnership supported GradBridge’s request to the state Council on Development Finance for up to $787,500 in grant funding from the Delaware Strategic Fund. The package includes a Jobs Performance Grant of up to $780,000 and a Capital Expenditure Grant of up to $7,500.
The grants are performance-based, meaning the money depends on GradBridge meeting its job creation and investment commitments.
Building a fintech ecosystem
The state’s fintech strategy has been developing around several connected goals: attracting high-growth financial technology companies, building a talent pipeline through the University of Delaware, creating space for startups and corporate innovation teams, and using Delaware’s position as a corporate and financial services center to shape the future of digital finance.
At UD’s STAR Campus, the FinTech Innovation Hub is envisioned as an anchor for that work. Its long-term plan includes research, degree pathways, bootcamps, apprenticeships, incubator space and partnerships among universities, companies and government. It also includes a focus on financial equity, including technology that can improve access to financial services for low- and moderate-income communities.
GradBridge fits several parts of that vision. It is a fintech company tied to Delaware’s lending and financial services expertise. It is creating high-wage professional jobs. And its business model is centered on expanding access to education financing for students who might otherwise be turned away by traditional lenders.
From planning to business growth
For Newark, the headquarters also adds another employer to the region’s growing innovation economy, building on the larger effort to make the area around UD, STAR Campus and Delaware Technology Park a hub for research-driven business growth.
For Delaware, the announcement is a reminder that economic development often takes years to mature. The state has spent years trying to connect its traditional strengths in banking, corporate law and financial services with newer opportunities in technology, data analytics and digital finance. GradBridge’s decision suggests that long-term strategy may be starting to produce the kind of companies and jobs state leaders hoped it would attract.
Delaware Prosperity Partnership, the state’s public-private economic development organization, said it has worked with GradBridge as the company developed its business plan, headquarters strategy and market expansion plans.
GradBridge says its mission is to help students who have already made progress toward a degree but need additional financing to graduate. The company describes its goal as turning loan denials into “graduation success stories” by helping students close funding gaps that could otherwise interrupt their education.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Finalists for Kansas Supreme Court vacancy willing to stand for election if amendment passes
description: Applicants for Kansas Supreme Court vacancy commit to campaigning for reelection if amendment to Kansas Constitution passes to force direct elections.
text:
Finalists for a vacancy on the Kansas Supreme Court are prepared to campaign in direct elections if voters in August decide to amend the Kansas Constitution. The six current justices, starting back row left, are Melissa Taylor Standridge, K.J. Wall and Larkin Walsh, and front row left, Dan Biles, Eric Rosen and Caleb Stegall. (Kansas Reflector screen capture of Kansas Supreme Court image)TOPEKA — Johnson County District Judge Robert Wonnell gave thought when applying for a vacancy on the Kansas Supreme Court to the proposed constitutional amendment that could transform the selection of justices serving on the state’s highest court.
He said no one should expect him to transform into a foot-stomping candidate eager to battle rivals with attack ads and make promises about the outcome of issues before the court.
“If I were selected to serve on the Supreme Court, and if the process were to change, I don’t know that I am capable or could become a political animal,” he said.
The amendment on the Aug. 4 ballot would erase the current merit-selection system in place since 1958. The process has relied on a nine-member Supreme Court Nominating Commission to interview applicants and submit a list of finalists to governors. The existing approach in Kansas requires Supreme Court justices to stand for retention after serving one year on the bench. If a majority of votes are cast to retain a justice, that individual remains for a term of six years.
The constitutional amendment advanced by the Republican-led House and Senate would require Supreme Court justices to be chosen through direct election. The commission, with a majority of members selected by attorneys, would no longer have a voice in picking Supreme Court justices.
Wonnell, appointed to the district court in 2015 by Republican Gov. Sam Brownback through the merit-based system, was among three finalists recommended in May by the commission to Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly to assume the seat created by retirement of former Chief Justice Marla Luckert.
“I think that I would discuss the independence of the judiciary,” Wonnell said. “I would be able to present what I have done. But as far as any type of engagement of an opponent or something like that, I don’t see myself ever looking toward discrediting anyone else.”
The nonpartisan commission endorsed Wonnell, Johnson County District Judge Chris Jayaram of Lenexa and Douglas County District Judge Carl Folsom of Lawrence from among seven applicants. Kelly appointed Folsom and Jayaram as district court judges within the past five years.
The 60-day window for Kelly to make the Supreme Court pick means a new justice could be appointed prior to the August vote on the constitutional amendment.
Jayaram, who received the broadest support among members of the nominating commission, said he would never fit the mold of a politician, even if compelled to seek election to the Supreme Court.
“I don’t think I would be a good politician because I like to pride myself on looking at both sides of an issue and trying to make the decision,” he said. “I don’t think that fits neatly into a politician’s box. Frankly, I think it doesn’t serve the judicial branch well to have to be put into that kind of box, where the perception might be that you are beholden to people who might donate to a campaign or a particular interest group or a position.”
He said open elections for Supreme Court justices could weaken public confidence in the idea of an impartial judiciary. Key legislative advocates of the amendment argued direct elections were needed to alter the Supreme Court’s view on abortion regulation and public school spending.
Folsom, who has never sought political office, said if appointed to the Supreme Court and if the constitution was changed he would respect the will of voters and file as a candidate.
“I’m prepared to do that if that’s the law and that’s where the people of Kansas say that they want their justices selected,” he said.
Other applicants for the vacancy on the Supreme Court likewise indicated a willingness to become part of the political process — if necessary.
Kansas Board of Tax Appeals Chair Kristen Wheeler of Wichita, who was among candidates not chosen as a finalist, said she was prepared to build upon her bipartisan relationships to advance prospects at the ballot box. If a member of the Supreme Court, she said, she would fight to hold the job.
“I’m not afraid of running. I’ve run many marathons. Even some ultramarathons, but the reality is that I want this position. I want it badly,” she said.
Lawrence attorney Meryl Carver-Allmond, who also applied for the Supreme Court opening, said she could warm to the idea of stumping for votes.
“I will say I’m not a natural politician. I would call myself more of an appellate nerd than someone that gets out and would be on the campaign trail. But, if it came to that, I would of course be willing to take on the role,” she said.
The prospect of engaging in election campaigns as a Supreme Court justice played into the process of deciding whether to apply for the vacancy, said Douglas County District Judge Amy Hanley.
Hanley said members of the judicial branch understood it was part of the ethical code of judges and justices to set aside personal agendas when deciding cases.
“The judicial canons make it very clear that we are to separate our personal opinions,” she said. “A judge may not allow any personal, political, family, financial or religious view to impact your decision.”
Molly McMurray Gordon, a federal prosecutor in Wichita and applicant for the Supreme Court seat, held a similar view: “Anyone who really wants to do this job, and would do a good job at it, does not want to be a politician.”
She added: “Politicians go out there and talk about the policies that they want. They make promises about the things that they would do. That’s not the role of a Supreme Court justice.”

title: Delaware Museum of Nature & Science camps mix dinosaurs, physics, space and fun!
description: Camps give children a chance to build independence, confidence and friendships in a lower-pressure setting than the classroom WILMINGTON — Delaware families looking for summer programs that mix fun with science can choose from a wide range of camp experiences at the Delaware Museum of Nature and Science, where this year’s lineup includes dinosaurs, outer spa[...]
text:
Camps give kids independence, confidence, friendships, and hands‑on learning in a low‑pressure environment where they can try new things without grades or judgment. Photo courtesy of the Delaware Museum of Nature and Science
Camps give children a chance to build independence, confidence and friendships in a lower-pressure setting than the classroom
WILMINGTON — Delaware families looking for summer programs that mix fun with science can choose from a wide range of camp experiences at the Delaware Museum of Nature and Science, where this year’s lineup includes dinosaurs, outer space, animal habitats, physics, forensics and even the science behind “gross” body functions.
The museum’s 2026 summer camp season is designed for children from 6 months to 14 years old, with programs divided by age group and format. Offerings include one-hour caregiver-and-child sessions for the youngest learners, half-day camps for ages 4 to 6, full-day camps for ages 5 to 8, and STEAM workshops for older campers ages 9 to 14.
The result is a summer schedule that gives families multiple entry points, whether they are introducing a toddler to nature activities for the first time or looking for a more advanced workshop for a middle school student interested in science, engineering or museums.
For parents, the value of summer camp goes beyond keeping children busy while school is out. Camps give children a chance to build independence, confidence and friendships in a lower-pressure setting than the classroom. Museum, nature and science camps also give children hands-on ways to learn by touching, building, experimenting and asking questions — activities that can strengthen curiosity, creativity and problem-solving. Because camps are structured but not driven by grades or tests, children also get room to try new things, make mistakes, work with others and build resilience.
A first camp experience for toddlers
The youngest program, Summer Camp for Tiny Explorers, is open to children ages 6 months to 4 years with a caregiver. The one-hour sessions run Wednesdays, June 10 through Aug. 19, or Thursdays, June 11 through Aug. 20, from 9 to 10 a.m.
The museum describes the program as a hands-on experience built around nature activities, counting, sorting, outdoor exploration, art, music and movement.
For many families, the toddler program offers an easy first step into camp life because children attend with a caregiver while still getting the benefit of a structured group experience.
Shorter days for younger campers
For preschool and early elementary children, the museum offers half-day camps for ages 4 to 6 from 9 a.m. to noon.
Themes include We Love Dinosaurs, Feats of Flight and Galaxy and Beyond, giving younger campers a chance to explore fossils, flying creatures and space in shorter sessions.
The half-day format can be a good fit for children who are ready for more independence but may not yet be ready for a full day away from home.
Full-day camps explore science through play
Full-day camps run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and are offered for ages 5 to 6 and 7 to 8.
The schedule includes topics such as Animal Architects, where children learn how animals build structures; Sensational Senses, which looks at how people and animals use their senses; Extreme Earth, focused on earthquakes, hurricanes and volcanoes; Mesozoic Monsters, centered on dinosaurs; and Outer Space Odyssey, which explores planets, moons and stars.
Other full-day camps take a more playful approach to science. Grossology invites younger campers to learn about burps, farts and other body functions, while Mystery at the Museum introduces ages 7 to 8 to basic forensic science as they work to solve a museum-themed mystery.
The mix of themes gives children a chance to explore serious science through activities designed to feel like adventure, discovery and play.
STEAM workshops for older children
Older campers can take part in STEAM workshops for ages 9 to 14.
Those include Mindcraft, which connects the Minecraft world to the natural world; Pocket Monsters & Real-Life Creatures, which looks at real animals that inspire fictional creatures; Phantastic Physics, where campers investigate matter and energy while creating a Rube Goldberg-style contraption; and Creating a Museum, which gives campers a behind-the-scenes look at museum work.
The workshops are designed for children who are ready for deeper exploration and more complex projects, with topics that connect science, technology, engineering, art and math.
Extended care and lunch options
The museum also offers practical options for working parents. Extended care is available for an additional fee and must be purchased in advance.
For full-day camps and STEAM workshops, morning care is offered from 8 to 9 a.m., and afternoon care is available from 4 to 5:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday. There is no after care on Fridays.
Campers attending full-day programs or workshops must bring lunch with an ice pack or pre-purchase lunch from the museum’s Rest, Relax, Recharge Café. Lunches through the café include a sandwich option and add-ons, with purchasing information provided to families before camp begins.
Scholarships available for qualifying families
The programs also include a scholarship option. Limited scholarships are available for 2026 school day off and summer camps for families who qualify.
According to the museum, eligible families must be in the EBT program and submit an approval letter. Scholarships cover 85% of the base camp cost, not including before or after care.
Registration and safety information
The museum says safety protocols are built into its programming and that staff monitor guidance from the Centers for Disease Control, the state of Delaware and the American Camp Association.
Families are also required to complete medical forms that identify allergies and other health or personal information, although the museum notes that because camps take place in a public space, it cannot guarantee an allergen-free environment.
Registration is available through the museum’s website. Some programs may sell out, and the museum notes that camps are subject to cancellation if minimum registration is not met or if other unforeseen circumstances arise.
If You Go
What: Delaware Museum of Nature and Science summer campsWhere: 4840 Kennett Pike, WilmingtonAges: 6 months to 14 years old, depending on programPrograms: Tiny Explorers, half-day camps, full-day camps and STEAM workshopsCost: Tiny Explorers starts at $10.50 for eligible members and $25 for non-member children; half-day camps are $185 for members and $230 for non-members; full-day camps and STEAM workshops are $315 for members and $355 for non-members.More information: delmns.org/programs/camps/

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Canceled ‘Cancer Alley’ documentary screening in St. John will move forward amid public backlash
description: A screening of a documentary about chemical pollution in St. John the Baptist Parish will finally move forward after it was abruptly canceled months ago due to what the event’s organizers said was pressure from the parish president. The reversal came several days after a Verite News story highlighted what free speech advocates and environmental […]
text:
Cattle graze in a pasture next to the Denka Performance Elastomer facility in LaPlace, where U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A screening of a documentary about chemical pollution in St. John the Baptist Parish will finally move forward after it was abruptly canceled months ago due to what the event’s organizers said was pressure from the parish president.
The reversal came several days after a Verite News story highlighted what free speech advocates and environmental groups criticized as censorship by Parish President Jaclyn Hotard, who has denied giving a direct order to cancel the late February screening of “The Big Sea” at a parish-owned theater.
The St. John Theatre’s board president, Sterling Snowdy, said in a letter that he had “misinterpreted” Hotard’s concerns about the event, which had been approved by the nonprofit board in December but was scrapped immediately after discussions with Hotard in late January.
“The theatre interpreted [Hotard’s] comments as a suggestion that the screening of a documentary or film could fall beyond (or outside) the contractual terms of our current lease,” Snowdy, a 40th Judicial District Court judge, wrote in a May 27 letter to Tulane University’s First Amendment Clinic, which represented Concerned Citizens of St. John, the group that had applied to screen the film.
A few days after the Verite story was published, the board “reexamined [Hotard’s] comments” and reversed its decision, Snowdy wrote.
“We would be delighted to screen the documentary,” he added.
The event is now scheduled for June 19 to coincide with Juneteenth festivities in the majority-Black parish.
“This feels wonderful,” said Tish Taylor, a member of Concerned Citizens. “It’s wonderful to have our rights respected, and to be able to use the freedoms we are guaranteed in the Constitution.”
St. John the Baptist Parish President Jaclyn Hotard.
Contacted on Monday, Hotard declined to say what concerns she had about the event or how screening a film at the venue, which was built as a movie theater nearly 100 years ago, might conflict with the board’s lease.
She directed questions to Snowdy, saying in a text that she “can’t answer for him.” Snowdy has not responded to requests for comment, nor has the theater’s manager, who in January told the Concerned Citizens that Hotard “vetoed” the screening.

Concerned Citizens of St. John the Baptist Parish will screen “The Big Sea” on June 19 at the St. John Theatre, 115 W. 4th St., Reserve. The event will begin with a reception at 6 p.m. and the screening at 7 p.m. A panel discussion will follow. The event is free. For information, see the Concerned Citizens website.  

“The Big Sea” explores the links between the global surfing industry and air pollution in Reserve, a mostly poor, Black community in St. John. It takes aim at Denka, a chemical plant near Reserve that was the nation’s only producer of chloroprene, a key ingredient in the neoprene wetsuits worn by surfers worldwide. Denka closed the plant last year partly due to pressures from federal regulators, which had determined that the facility posed cancer risks to St. John residents and imperiled the health of children attending a nearby school.
The closure angered some local leaders, including Hotard, who credited the facility with boosting St. John’s economy. The parish, which sits along the Mississippi River between New Orleans and Baton Rouge, was once dominated by plantations but is now a hub for the chemical industry.
“The Big Sea” was released to critical acclaim last year as Denka began suspending operations. The documentary earned more than a dozen awards at international film festivals and attracted coverage from several magazines and newspapers, but it had yet to have a public showing in the community in which much of it was filmed.
Taylor said the theater was initially supportive of the screening. The facility, which the parish purchased and renovated in 1980, typically has only a few bookings each month. Its May offerings included a talent show, a children’s theater workshop and a tea party.
Hotard’s involvement in the screening’s cancellation seemed to follow a pattern of behavior, Taylor said.
“She’s a bully, and this is how bullies act,” Taylor said.
First elected parish president in 2019, Hotard has repeatedly clashed with Concerned Citizens and other environmental groups over Denka and other industrial projects. Court filings in 2024 revealed she used violent language against activists opposing a now-defunct grain terminal and that her family stood to profit through a related land deal. Last year, a jury cleared Hotard of allegations that she restricted activists’ speech during parish meetings.
The theater’s manager, Amy Wombles, initially said Hotard “personally made the call” to cancel the event.
“We regret that we must inform you that Parish President Jaclyn Hotard has vetoed the screening of The Big Sea documentary at St. John Theatre,” Wombles wrote in an email to Taylor in late January. “The Parish President and the Sheriff have the authority to close any event at St. John Theatre for a variety of reasons.”
When Hotard declined to give a reason, Concerned Citizens enlisted the help of Tulane’s First Amendment Clinic, which sent letters and emails to Hotard in late January. According to the clinic’s lawyers, Hotard repeatedly declined to discuss the issue. In March, the clinic sent a letter to parish council members calling the cancellation a violation of Taylor’s rights.
“Your continued infringement of Ms. Taylor’s constitutional rights leaves the Parish open to further litigation, at St. John taxpayers’ expense,” the clinic warned.
Hotard didn’t address her role in the cancellation until after Verite News published a story about the issue on May 14. While she denied directly ordering the cancellation, Hotard would not discuss her conversations with the theater’s management nor explain why she waited more than three months to respond publicly.
She appeared to place the blame on the theater, telling Verite that Wombles and Snowdy “should set the record straight” and had put the parish in “potential liability.”
Taylor credits Verite’s coverage and the resulting outcry for finally getting the screening back on track.
“Until your article, they had ignored everything we’d done,” she told a Verite reporter. “Public exposure is what did it. [Hotard] has an image. She cares what the public thinks. And once the public knew, all of a sudden things start to happen.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: In a warming Arctic, gray whales struggle to find nourishment
description: Raymond, Washington — Doug Nussbaum is a retired logger whose morning rituals include a walk down to the bluff behind his house that overlooks a bend in the Willapa River. He is never quite sure just what he will spot — ducks, bald eagles and sometimes seals and sea lions pursuing salmon. On April 1, […]
text:
A gray whale and her healthy calf swim in the Pacific waters off Washington. Gray whale calf counts have plummeted, and last year were the lowest on record, according to NOAA Fisheries estimates. 
(Image courtesy of NOAA Fisheries/ Alaska Fisheries Science Center)Raymond, Washington — Doug Nussbaum is a retired logger whose morning rituals include a walk down to the bluff behind his house that overlooks a bend in the Willapa River.
He is never quite sure just what he will spot — ducks, bald eagles and sometimes seals and sea lions pursuing salmon. On April 1, he heard a breeching sound, then was stunned to see a gray whale — some 35 feet in length — swimming in circles.
This whale, skinny and malnourished, had gone catastrophically astray on a spring migration that, for most grays, starts in calving lagoons in Mexico and ends in summer feeding grounds off Alaska and northeast Russia.
For some two hours, the whale held in the bend, about 12 river miles inland from a saltwater bay. As the tide shifted, the whale made a brief push downstream, then reversed course to swim even farther upstream, lingering several days before dying in a shallow, narrow stretch of the river strewn with woody debris.
 “I don’t know what turned him around. I think he knew he wasn’t going to make it, and was looking for a place to die,” Nussbaum said.

This whale is one of more than 900 eastern North Pacific grays that have been found dead along the shorelines of Mexico, Canada and the United States since 2019. Malnourishment was often a factor. Many more perished at sea as the estimated population plummeted during the past seven years from a high of more than 27,000 whales in 2016 to less than 13,000 last year.
There also has been an implosion in gray whale births. Last year’s estimated count was the lowest since federal surveys began back in 1994.
Some marine scientists first thought the gray whale population was undergoing a cyclical population downturn after a big expansion that had strained their food resources. But the whales have not bounced back, and these researchers now assign an important role in the whales’ decline to 21st century shifts in temperatures, currents and winter ice cover that have reduced their foraging success in the northern seas.
“What has changed. The obvious answer is the climate,” wrote Joshua Stewart, an assistant professor at Oregon State University’s Marine Mammal Institute, in an October 2025 article published in the Journal of Marine Science with four co-authors. “The Arctic is the most rapidly warming region on the planet…”
A fading food source off Alaska
For grays, a favored food source is amphipods, a small crustacean that whales once found in huge abundance in the Chirikov Basin, a swath of the northern Bering Sea between Russia and Alaska. 
Amphipods thickly carpeted much of the basin’s sea floor. They clustered together in mud tubes that allowed them to filter feed on decaying bits of algae, which grows on the underside of sea ice then falls to the bottom.
In dives, a gray whale could suck up more than 2,000 pounds a day of the amphipods from these tubes with the aid of their baleen that filtered out sand. This protein-packed feed helped the whales build up the fat reserves they needed to power their marathon migrations back and forth to Mexican waters.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

“It was this really rich area — the wheat field of the Arctic for them,” said Jacqueline Grebmeier, a University of Maryland environmental scientist who has spent more than three decades researching marine life in the northern Bering Sea.
But in the 21st century, accelerated Arctic warming reduced winter ice. In some years, it changed the timing of the melt. All of that reduced the amount of algae that reached the seafloor to nourish the amphipods.
The survival of these Chirikov Basin crustaceans also was undermined by increased current flows of warmer waters from the northern Bering Sea into the Arctic. This swept away much of the silt that the amphipods needed to build their tube structures, according to Grebmeier.
By 2010, the amphipod population in the Chirkov Basin had collapsed to only 9% of the 1984 population, according to a master’s thesis by Brian Marx, a research colleague of Grebmeier who analyzed decades of northern Bering Sea survey records.
Amphipods, a favored food of the gray whales, once carpeted the bottom of the Chirikov Basin in the northern Bering Sea. But by 2010, they had gone into sharp decline in the basin that once was a prime foraging area for the whales. (Photo courtesy of Brian Marx)
Many gray whales responded to the radical changes in the basin by pushing farther north into the Arctic’s Chukchi and Beaufort Sea, which amid the Arctic warming had a greater inflow of nutrient rich waters that helped to support more sea life.  These gray whales could find some amphipods but also had a more varied diet, which likely included krill, a free-swimming crustecean, according to Grebmeier and other marine researchers.
Surprisingly, in the aftermath of the Chirikov Basin amphipod bust documented by Marx, the gray whales initially appear to have thrived, expanding to record high levels in 2016. 
But beginning in 2019, amid a severe marine heat wave that reached deep into northern waters, gray whales struggled to find enough food in the Arctic to fuel their long annual migration — even when they journeyed into the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas.
Since then, biologists on coastal surveys and in Mexico birthing lagoons have tallied increases in skinny whales with misshapen “peanut” heads that are marked by a severe loss of fat that leaves a concave depression behind their skulls.
“The common denominator is basically just not enough body fat, not enough oil in the fatty tissue that they live off — and they’re just running out of steam,” said Steve Swartz, a marine mammal scientist who has spent decades studying the gray whales in their Mexican calving grounds.
As of the end of May, 25 gray whales had washed ashore along Washington’s waterways during the spring migration period. Most of these whales had poor body condition, including the Willapa River gray, according to Cascadia Research Collective, a Washington-based scientific organization authorized by federal fishery officials to conduct necropsies.
The gray whale carcasses are sometimes left to decompose. Three weeks after its death, the Willapa River gray remains were decaying along a river bank near a boat ramp.
This gray whale carcass washed up on a beach north of Ocean Shores, Washington, one of 25 that  have been found dead along the state’s shorelines as of the end of May 2026. (Photo by Hal Bernton)
Fifty miles to the northeast, in the resort community of Ocean Shores, Washington, city officials opted for a different approach to disposing of three dead grays that washed up on a prime stretch of beach. They hired an excavator crew to attach cables to the whales, then dragged the carcasses into nearby sand dunes and buried them in pits.
“This is specialized work. They charged us $1,500 per whale,” said Scott Andersen, Ocean Shore’s city administrator. 
Hunting the grays
In the 19th and early 20th centuries, commercial whalers targeted grays largely for their oil, which was used in lamps and lubricants, as well as baleen that ended up in corsets, umbrellas and even buggy whips.
The hunts nearly wiped out the eastern North Pacific whale populations. By the 1930s, researchers estimate that just a few thousand, or less, remained, the risk of extinction prompted an international agreement to end commercial whaling. 
These gray whales, in the decades that followed, staged a remarkable resurgence. By 1994, with their population estimated at more than 20,000, they were removed from the U.S. Endangered Species Act listing in one of the most notable marine conservation successes of the last century.
Under the regulation of the International Whaling Commission, subsistence hunting of grays by the Russian indigenous people of the Chukotka region has been allowed to continue.
During the past quarter century, the Russians have averaged 125 whales landed each year, according to Russian reports to the commission.
I witnessed one of these hunts during a reporting trip to Chukotka in 2000, when relations between the U.S. and Russia had improved enough to travel there via a brief charter flight from the northwest Alaska town of Nome.
Roman Nosukak levels his harpoon at the 10-ton gray whale to put another float on it in Checkekuyum Strait during a subsistence hunt in 2000. Floats prevent the whale’s escape, tire it so it can be shot with rifles and home-made whale bombs. During the past quarter century, Russian indigenous hunters have taken an average of 125 gray whales to help feed villagers in the Chukotka region. (Photo by Alan Berner/ Seattle Times)
The Novoe Chaplino villagers were in dire straits, lacking many of the foodstuffs that had been delivered during the Soviet era. They were able to reclaim their subsistence roots with some assistance from Alaska Inupiat whalers who provided darting guns and projectiles.
The gray whales remain an important source of food for the coastal villages of Chukotka, according to Russian reports to the International Whaling Commission. But in recent years, as the gray whale population has tumbled, some U.S. scientists have expressed concerns about the impacts of whaling, along with other human activities, such as ship strikes and fishing gear entanglements.
They include Swartz and his Mexican colleagues who study the whales in Laguna San Ignacio, a major calving area that provides warm waters shielded from orca predators that roam further north. In these lagoons, gray whales breed — and after a year’ s gestation — give birth to calves that drink a high-fat milk that enables them to triple their weight before joining in the spring, north-bound migration.
During the past decade, Swartz observed huge reductions in the number of gray whales giving birth, along with increases in the numbers of skinny whales as well as those that appear to be a reasonable weight but do not bear calves.
That stark trend is also evident in the broader calf count conducted by NOAA Fisheries biologists at Piedras Blancas Lighthouse Station in central California, where they track calves migrating north each spring. In 2025, NOAA estimated there were just 85 calves — down nearly 95 percent from more than 1,500 estimated in 2015. This year, calf counts also are expected to be low.
“Let’s get real here,” Swartz said. “The whales are having a really rough time.”
Last August, Swartz, along with a Canadian and Mexican colleague, sent an open “letter of concern” to the International Whaling Commission urging a review of gray whale biology and their management.
That letter got a cool response from Dennis Litovka, a Russian scientist who directs the Chukotka Arctic Scientific Center and serves on the whaling commission’s scientific review committee. 
“We don’t accept and cannot support such (an) idea,” Litovka wrote in response to questions  from this reporter about the letter of concern. 
In his comments, Litovka wrote about the importance of gray whales to the Chukotka villagers and whalers with whom he had lived and worked “shoulder to shoulder.” He said that Russian scientists do not see dramatic changes in a Chukotka bay frequented by gray whales. As for quota reductions, they should be made “only very exceptionally,” and as a last resort if gray whale populations continue to decline, Litovka wrote. 
Litovka serves on the whaling commission’s science committee that in 2024 concluded that, despite the die off, the gray whale population can sustain the authorized hunt levels, currently a maximum of 840 whales over six years when a small number reserved for Washington’s Makah Indians are included. The scientists met last May for a meeting that included a gray whale review. But the commission is not scheduled to revisit the gray whale subsistence quota until 2030.
Foraging in the Pacific Northwest 
For decades, whale researchers have reported that some gray whales may opt out of the long migration to the Arctic to feed in other locations. They include more than 200 whales that spend much of their time foraging off northern California, Oregon, Washington, British Columbia and Southeast Alaska. 
A much smaller group ventures deep into Puget Sound to spend part of the year pursuing ghost shrimp in shallow coastal waters that turn to mudflats during low tide.
“We call it a high-risk feeding strategy because they may be a mile away from safe water, and as the tide goes out, they’ve got to get out before they get stranded,” said John Calambokidis, a senior research biologist at Cascadia Research Collective.
Other gray whales that forage in Pacific Northwest waters have become skilled, versatile foragers. They filter feed on crab larvae and skim feed through kelp beds for mysids, a shrimp-like crustacean.
Amid the overall decline of the gray whale population, the numbers feeding in the Pacific Northwest have been stable. 
“They have looked very good,” Jeff Harris, a NOAA Fisheries biologist who surveyed large areas of Northwest coastal waters frequented by the grays.
Some gray whales that have long fed in the Arctic are also trying to feed along the West Coast to gain an energy boost for their migration. Since 2018, there has been an increase in whales venturing into San Francisco Bay, where they are at high risk of getting killed by vessels. In an article published in April in the Frontiers of Marine Science, researchers identified 114 whales that entered between 2018 and 2025 and found that 18 of them later died within the bay. 
If conditions don’t improve in the Arctic, more whales may opt to feed in the Pacific Northwest. But the Pacific ocean off Oregon and Washington has a narrow continental shelf that limits the prime foraging for grays, so it’s not likely to provide enough food for a much larger gray whale population.
But another big climate event could soon make life more difficult for gray whales. As early as July, marine forecasters are expecting a powerful El Nino marked by weakening trade winds that would send warm Pacific waters to the West Coast and the Bering Sea.
El Ninos typically weaken, and sometimes curtail, nutrient-rich upwellings of cold water that are vital to the marine food chain that supports gray whales. This one, according to some models, could be one of the strongest on record. 
“I think it’s just going to shake up the whole ocean,” said Harris, the NOAA biologist. “A lot of species are going to be struggling.”
A gray whale that washed up dead in April on a beach in Seaside, Oregon undergoes a necropsy with a team authorized by NOAA Fisheries. The necropsy helps to determine a cause of death, and biologists noted a pinkish hue to blubber that could be a sign of malnutrition. (Photo by Hal Bernton)
