title: North Dakota energy research center brings back part of furloughed workforce
description: The University of North Dakota’s Energy and Environmental Research Center has started to bring back employees who were furloughed last month with more reinstatements possible as recently announced federal contracts are finalized.  An agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy announced May 22 will provide $25 million to the EERC over five years. That’s on[...]
text:
Charlie Gorecki, CEO of the Energy and Environmental Research Center, presents to the North Dakota Industrial Commission on Aug. 27, 2024. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)The University of North Dakota’s Energy and Environmental Research Center has started to bring back employees who were furloughed last month with more reinstatements possible as recently announced federal contracts are finalized. 
An agreement with the U.S. Department of Energy announced May 22 will provide $25 million to the EERC over five years. That’s on top of $36 million from the Department of Energy announced in early May. 
Research projects will include the Crack the Code 2.0 initiative aimed at getting more oil from shale formations such as the Bakken in North Dakota. 
EERC Executive Director Charlie Gorecki said the center is still negotiating the terms of these agreements with the Department of Energy. 
“We are aiming to have the negotiations completed as early as the end of June, at which time we can start working on those projects,” Gorecki said in an email. 
North Dakota energy research center cuts affect 40 staff

UND confirmed May 7 that EERC was cutting 27 positions. Another 13 employees were furloughed, meaning the positions could be reinstated.
Gorecki said two of the furloughed employees have been brought back. EERC “will continue to recall employees as project work allows,” Gorecki said. 
UND said the cutbacks were because of funding delays. EERC gets much of its funding from federal agencies, such as the Department of Energy. 
Kyle Haustveit, undersecretary at the Department of Energy, said in an interview that the department paused funding for some projects after the 2024 election while they reviewed them and ensured the funding was aligned with the goals of President Donald Trump’s administration. 
He said that the department is “absolutely back on track” with funding research projects.
“We’re moving forward with the majority of projects that were paused for review,” Haustveit said while attending last month’s Williston Basin Petroleum Conference in Bismarck. 
Gorecki said other projects could also help bring back furloughed workers. 
“We are continuously working with our partners on new projects and proposals,” Gorecki said. 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jacob Orledge contributed to this report.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Coalition asks state leaders to immediately pause WV school closures as lawmakers mull funding fix
description: A coalition of families, educators and community members has called for an immediate pause on school closures in West Virginia so lawmakers have time to address the state’s antiquated school funding formula. West Virginia has seen an accelerated wave of school closures in the last few years mostly due to the state’s declining population. During […]
text:
Lockers in a Kanawha County school in West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/West Virginia Watch)A coalition of families, educators and community members has called for an immediate pause on school closures in West Virginia so lawmakers have time to address the state’s antiquated school funding formula.
West Virginia has seen an accelerated wave of school closures in the last few years mostly due to the state’s declining population.
During this past school year alone, 19 schools were proposed for closure. Since 2011, 139 West Virginia public schools have closed and 71% of those have been elementary schools, according to a news release from the Together for Public Schools WV Coalition.
Verdunville Elementary in Logan County closed last year due to enrollment decline and a rockslide that impacted the school.
“Verdunville Elementary closing has been exhausting for me and my child. The distance to the new school makes it difficult to participate in events. We were left with a lot of unanswered questions during the closure process, and the community is afraid the building is just going to sit there and rot,” said Billy Reeves, a parent in Logan County.
Together for Public Schools WV Coalition said that more than 85% of students attend public schools. 
“Across the state, closure decisions are moving forward rapidly, often without time for meaningful community input, clear financial justification or adequate plans to support impacted students,” the coalition wrote.
They also noted closures result in longer bus rides for students.
Geary Elementary Middle School in Roane County will close at the end of the year along with another county school. The school district is experiencing financial issues due to a significant drop in student enrollment.
Dustin Vaughan is a Roane County resident whose daughter attends Geary Elementary Middle School.
“There are several in her class that don’t have reliable transportation and the bus won’t even be stopping at their house … they don’t know what they’re going to do,” Vaughan said. “A lot of these parents have to drive two or three miles to meet the bus. We understand that smaller counties are losing population, but we also understand that smaller schools and smaller class sizes are better for the kids. Why don’t we come up with some base amount of funding for each rural school to keep them open?”
Together for Public Schools WV also called on state leaders to create a stabilization fund so districts can access to prevent or reverse school closures while lawmakers consider revamping the school funding formula. 
House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay, reads over the report while analysts with the RAND corporation present the information on Jan. 14, 2026, at the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Lawmakers looking at special education funding after no action this year
West Virginia uses a seven-step formula to determine how much state funding goes to county school systems based on factors including the number of students enrolled. 
While the state’s population is declining, the number of special education students is increasing, leading to tight budgets for many districts. Required special education costs, like providing one-on-one aides to help with feeding or toileting, have forced districts into millions of dollars of debt.
West Virginia schools are 2,685.92 school personnel positions over formula, according to the state education department, and the state has seen another year of widespread teacher and staff cuts. Counties will use local funds, if available, to avoid making job cuts. 
A recent $114,000 study from the RAND Corporation, paid for by the House of Delegates, suggested that the state give more money to special education services to improve school budgets.
While lawmakers came into the 2026 legislative session with plans to revamp the formula, the session ended in March without any of those measures making it to the governor’s desk for consideration. 
House Education Chairman Joe Statler, said during House-only meetings earlier this month that bolstering special education funding will be an ongoing focus, MetroNews reported. 
“We’re far from the end of this. We’re just starting this race, and we are committed. I think I can safely say that (for) the committee, this is one of the top issues that is before us,” said Statler, R-Monongalia. “I know that the money is always going to be an issue, but we will work through and around that problem.”
A proposed special education funding bill introduced in the Senate earlier this year was estimated to cost $45.9 million.
In the House, a proposed broader update to the entire funding formula would have cost $214 million, causing a hangup for lawmakers. 
“While lawmakers may need time to fully develop their plan to update the funding formula, students and communities should not suffer while they wait,” Together for Public Schools WV said. “Communities and school district leaders deserve time to plan responsibly and have a real voice in decisions that will impact generations of West Virginians.”
The RAND report commissioned by House members also recommended West Virginia make changes to its broad school voucher program, the Hope Scholarship. Lawmakers allocated nearly $300 million toward this program during the legislative session. 
The program is now available for all K-12 students for the first time since the program launched in 2021. The RAND report recommended against this expansion, saying, “that such an expansion would inefficiently subsidize private school tuition for many families who would have chosen private schools regardless.”

text:
The Arkansas Advocate team on the steps of the state Capitol (from left): Editor-in-Chief Andrew DeMillo, reporters Ainsley Platt and Tess Vrbin, and Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda. (Photo by Sonny Albarado)Arkansas Advocate staff won five first-place awards, including for its series exploring overcrowding in the state prison system, in the 2026 Arkansas Press Women Professional Communications Contest over the weekend.
The Advocate’s “Overcrowded” series by Deputy Editor Antoinette Grajeda and reporters Tess Vrbin and Ainsley Platt won first place in the in-depth reporting category. The four-part series last year explored the consequences of the state’s growing prison population.
The awards were announced Saturday at an event in Conway. There were 338 entries in the contest.
Vrbin won first place in the news story category for online publications for her story examining concerns about a state law promoting “restorative reproductive medicine.”
Vrbin also won second place in continuing coverage for her writing on library restrictions, second place in health for her coverage of maternity ward shortages and second place in social issues for her story on the origin of a law limiting access to LGBTQ+ books in school libraries.
Grajeda won first place in continuing coverage for her coverage of immigration and first place for personality profile for her story about Ann Cornwell, the first woman to serve as Arkansas Senate secretary. Grajeda also won honorable mention in the education category for her coverage of the installation of Ten Commandments posters at the University of Arkansas.
Platt won first place for government or politics coverage for her story looking at the delays in fixing a Department of Corrections wastewater plant.
Former editor-in-chief Sonny Albarado won honorable mention in personal opinion column.
The Advocate, which launched in 2022, is a nonpartisan, independent newsroom covering Arkansas government and politics. It’s an affiliate of States Newsroom, the nation’s largest state-focused nonprofit news organization. Advocate stories are available for free online and available at no cost for other news outlets to republish. The Advocate’s work is supported by grants and donations.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama Democrats had a good primary. But challenges remain.
description: It’s not hard to understand Alabama Democrats’ delight with the May 19 results. Team Blue increased its share of the total primary vote to its highest number since 2006 (the last time Democrats led voting in any Alabama primary). Democrats got good turnout in Jefferson and Montgomery counties and the Black Belt, their core regions. […]
text:
Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear speaks to an audience while Former U.S. Sen. and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Doug Jones listens on May 20, 2026. Alabama Democrats nearly doubled their overall vote in the May 19 primary. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)It’s not hard to understand Alabama Democrats’ delight with the May 19 results.
Team Blue increased its share of the total primary vote to its highest number since 2006 (the last time Democrats led voting in any Alabama primary). Democrats got good turnout in Jefferson and Montgomery counties and the Black Belt, their core regions. Even better for the party, Democrats took a majority of the ballots in Madison, Mobile and Tuscaloosa counties.
“Democrats last night overperformed in our elections,” Doug Jones, the party’s gubernatorial nominee, said the day after the election. “That was a big number. We increased the number of Democratic votes significantly, 15% or more. And we did that without spending a lot of money.”
It was actually better than Jones said, an increase of over 20% over 2022. The number of people taking a Democratic ballot nearly doubled from four years ago.
But first, a few things to consider.
First, 2022 was a disaster for the party. Democrats had a poor slate of statewide candidates, many first-timers with no constituencies. They neither spent nor raised money and couldn’t harness outrage over the Dobbs decision.
Just 189,000 Alabamians voted in the Democratic primary that year. This year’s turnout — up to 365,000 — means the party should avoid one peculiar trend in 2022, when Black Belt Democrats found themselves in tight races. 
Still, 58% of primary voters cast a ballot in the GOP primary. It’s worth pointing out that Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville got more votes in the effectively uncontested GOP primary for that office than all the Democratic gubernatorial candidates put together.  
The primary electorate also differs from the voters who come out for the general election. If those groups were the same in the 2017 special U.S. Senate election, Roy Moore could be in the middle of his second full term as Alabama’s U.S. senator. He’s not. Jones won that contest, even though fewer than 30% of primary voters that year took a Democratic ballot.    


 

	 The real game starts when the competitors are set. And one has to make a pitch all over again. Here again, Tuberville has an advantage. As of May 21, the U.S. senator had $9.4 million on hand, a figure that will grow over the next several months.  Jones had about $1.1 million as of May 18.
Tuberville may have to spend all that money if President Donald Trump, for whom he wants to rename Presidents Day, remains unpopular. The Economist had him underwater with all voters in Alabama last week. And Jones has won a previous statewide race. But a cash advantage like that could allow Tuberville to set the tone for the campaign. And with his hateful views of immigrants, Muslims and Black Alabamians, it might be a discordant one.
Democrats also have to face the vertical cliff of straight-ticket voting. Many voters check a party box without scrutinizing the candidates. In a state with racially polarized voting, where most white Alabamians vote for Republicans and most Black Alabamians vote for Democrats, that’s an advantage for Republicans. The state’s population is 64% white. 
And as of this writing, we don’t know if the U.S. Supreme Court will unleash more confusion in the state’s congressional races. Uncertainty over elections could hurt Republicans as much as Democrats. But Democrats have far less margin for error.
So Democrats in Alabama always get the bigger challenge. GOP strategy is straightforward: Turn out your voters.  
If Democrats have any hope of winning a statewide race? They must win the four urban counties and the Black Belt by large percentages. They also have to add Tuscaloosa County (doable) and Lee County (much less so). And if they pull that off, they still need Republican voters to stay home in key counties. If your strategy rests on your opponents’ blundering, you’re the underdog.

 
But numbers indicate there may be positive signs for Democrats.
Turnout in Republican-leaning counties generally fell or stayed flat over 2022. Most of the counties in the Wiregrass, a GOP bastion, saw turnout fall. Pike County (home of Troy University) saw an increase, but that was due to Democratic voting. It jumped from about 1,100 votes in 2022 to nearly 2,500 on May 19. Republican votes fell from almost 4,000 to 3,100.
Madison County, where Democrats have pinned a lot of their hopes, saw flat turnout but a shift from a primary electorate that was 81% GOP four years ago to one that was nearly 53% Democratic last month. That’s not a predictor of anything, but it’s the sort of trend Democrats hoping to pick up legislative seats around Huntsville want to see. And the fact that turnout snapped back in Jefferson and Montgomery – critical to anything Democrats want to do in November — will help.
Alabama remains a Republican state, but the May 19 primary showed that Alabama Democrats have a pulse. That won’t make the state purple. But it could mean more blue dots in the red sea of our state.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Editor’s notebook: The silence of Tennessee’s ‘statesmen’
description: Politically interested Tennesseans of a certain era often invoke the ghost of Howard Baker, longtime Republican U.S. senator, when they talk of statesmen and trends in the Tennessee GOP.  Baker, who served in the Senate from his 1966 election through 1984, was known as the “Great Conciliator” for his skill in brokering bipartisan deals and […]
text:
Former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen, photographed during his 2018 U.S. Senate run, won all 95 counties in his 2006 gubernatorial reelection race and remains highly-thought of in the state, bur rarely addresses controversial issues.(Photo by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)Politically interested Tennesseans of a certain era often invoke the ghost of Howard Baker, longtime Republican U.S. senator, when they talk of statesmen and trends in the Tennessee GOP. 
Baker, who served in the Senate from his 1966 election through 1984, was known as the “Great Conciliator” for his skill in brokering bipartisan deals and his commitment to civil discourse. He served as the ranking minority member on the committee investigating President Richard Nixon’s involvement in the Watergate scandal — a scandal that seems petty compared to those that have transpired in recent years. 
What would Baker, who died in 2014, say of politics today, ask pundits? 
Baker’s not around to opine, but there are several former U.S. senators and governors with plenty of political capital to expend, free to offer their opinions on state politics. 
Often cited as Tennessee statesmen of the current generation: Democratic former Vice-President Al Gore; former Govs. Phil Bredesen, a Democrat, and Bill Haslam, a Republican; and Republican former U.S. Sen. Lamar Alexander.
But it’s rare for any of the group to speak out on controversial issues. The Lookout reached out for comment on the state’s sudden mid-decade redistricting anyway. 
Former Vice President Al Gore, photographed during a May 1 climate event at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, called a move by the Tennessee General Assembly to redraw the state’s congressional districts to carve up a primarily Black district “a problem for democracy.” (Photo: Cassandra Stephenson/Tennessee Lookout)
Gore, who also served as U.S. representative and U.S. senator before being tapped to be President Bill Clinton’s veep, spoke with Lookout reporter Cassandra Stephenson during a recent interview and addressed the special legislative session in early May to redraw Tennessee’s congressional maps.
“The very idea that we have made enough — this is the Supreme Court’s apparent view — that we’ve made enough progress on the racial divide in America that now it’s time not only to stop any kind of remedial efforts, but also to try to criminalize any remedial efforts, you know, by labeling it DEI and condemning it and punishing people for even trying to address the obvious problems that we still have,” said Gore, who labeled the redistricting “a problem for democracy.” 
But redistricting isn’t the only Tennessee issue that calls for comment. Chief among others is the continued attempt to whitewash history. 
Alexander, who retired from the Senate in 2018, is promoting a new book about his 60 years in politics called “The Education of a Senator.” In a recent interview with The New York Times, says he wishes current senators would stand up to President Donald Trump, saying Trump has “steamrolled over a compliant Senate in his second term.”
The cynical will say that Alexander is making a bid to seal his legacy, but me, I appreciate that Alexander is speaking out, finally. When he was still in the Senate in Trump’s first term, he stymied Trump impeachment hearings, voted to confirm Betsy DeVos — a billionaire Trump supporter with no experience in education — as secretary of Education and argued Democratic senators should defer to the president. 
But as the saying goes, when you know better, you do better. 
Alexander offered a public statement recently when Knox County Schools banned the historical novel “Roots,” a move that again made national news for making Tennessee look stupid, before the school board issued a take back. The Pulitzer Prize-winning book detailing the horrors of slavery was named a state book in 2024 and was written by Alex Haley, who lived in Tennessee at several periods in his life, and a personal friend of Alexander’s. 
“Alex was a Tennessean, a frequent guest at the governor’s residence when we lived there. Our children knew him well. He told them stories from Roots,” Alexander said in a statement. “We don’t believe in canceling part of our history. We wanted our children to understand that the American Republic has never been a perfect union but that its greatness is that it has always struggled to reach noble goals.”
My efforts to reach Haslam and Bredesen were fruitless. 
The pair have a podcast called, “You Might Be Right,” sponsored by the Baker School of Policy and Public Affairs at the University of Tennessee. 
Bill Haslam, Tennessee’s immediate past governor, stays busy as chair of the 2030 Nashville Super Bowl and has a podcast with former Gov. Phil Bredesen, but offers little comment on current events. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In the podcast, which draws its title from one of Baker’s expressions, the pair discuss topics including the national debt, climate change, the future of separation of powers and charter schools. Haslam and Bredsen launched their first season with an episode titled, “Am I using my morals as a weapon or a gift?” 
More than half a dozen people, Republican and Democrat, have contacted me to ask my take on why neither of the former governors have made public statements about the recent redistricting, gerrymandering in general or hyperpartisanism. 
My guess is that they let their podcast, which draws on the notion of “civility,” do all the talking for them.
But Tennessee has a leadership void and a podcast isn’t enough. These days, when what passes for “leadership” in Tennessee often means parroting the mean-spirited talking points of Trump, including anti-immigrant rhetoric and name-calling, state residents dearly want to hear from the two men I often hear referred to as two of Tennessee’s best governors. 
Sure, both Haslam and Bredesen have done their time in the political barrel — both served as mayors, Haslam of Knoxville, Bredesen of Nashville, before becoming two-term governors — but neither have anything to lose. 
A mentor once told me that what’s last remembered is best remembered and the way for the current crop of former lawmakers to solidify their cred as statesmen isn’t through books or podcasts or resting on their past laurels: it’s by raising their voices now, at a time when the public arena and their former constituents would greatly benefit by hearing from leaders who are sane, moral and still popular.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Democratic voters to choose state Senate nominee in wide open Huntsville-area runoff
description: In a wide open seat in north Alabama, Democratic voters will choose their nominee for Senate District 2 in the June 16 primary runoff election. Democratic voters on May 19  narrowed their choice to Rudolph Drake, a Navy veteran, and Alex House, an academic advisor. Drake got 4,561 votes, about 36.6%, to House’s 4,221, about […]
text:
Democratic voters will choose between (left to right) Rudolph Drake of Madison and Alex House of Huntsville for the Democratic nomination for Senate District 2, a wide open seat in north Alabama. The pair advanced to the June 16 runoff, and the winner will face Republican John Roberts in November. (Photo of Drake by Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector and courtesy of House; graphic by Anna Barrett)In a wide open seat in north Alabama, Democratic voters will choose their nominee for Senate District 2 in the June 16 primary runoff election.
Democratic voters on May 19  narrowed their choice to Rudolph Drake, a Navy veteran, and Alex House, an academic advisor. Drake got 4,561 votes, about 36.6%, to House’s 4,221, about 33.9% of the total. A third candidate, Airbus pilot Guy Sotomayor, got the other 3,689 votes, about 29.6%, according to unofficial returns.
Senate District 2 covers the western part of Madison County and some of eastern Limestone County. The district is considered a priority race for the Alabama Democratic Party due to Huntsville’s growth over the last decade and its favorable demographics for the party. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Current Sen. Tom Butler, R-Madison, who is not seeking re-election, got 55.5% of the votes in 2022. In the 2024 presidential election, former Vice President Kamala Harris won the district by 0.1%, according to estimates by Madison County data analyst Jackson Hannan using precinct-level voting data.
The candidate with the most votes will face Republican John Roberts, a realtor, in November.
The candidates
Drake, 63, said in a phone interview Friday morning that voters should choose him because he has the leadership skills through the Navy to think strategically in the upper chamber.
“This job, I think, requires somebody who’s had some leadership experience,” he said. “You want to always think ahead, always want to think three to five steps ahead. What’s Plan A, what’s Plan B, what’s Plan C?”
If elected, plans to address the rising cost of living in Alabama, infrastructure and rising healthcare costs. He hopes to use the framework of existing programs, like before- and after-school programs, to address parts of the affordability issues Alabamians are facing.
Drake said he would also like to suspend the state’s 30-cent-per-gallon gas tax to provide Alabamians relief from increasing gas prices. According to AAA Gas Prices, the price per gallon of regular gas in Alabama is $4.02, as of Friday, up $1.27 from May 2025, and 39 cents from March 27 when Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones called for the suspension of the tax.
“Everything’s running hand-in-hand. You gotta have gas to go to work. You gotta be able to have some kind of healthcare for your kids, so it all really falls in line,” Drake said. 
House, 41, said in a phone interview Friday afternoon that while he agrees with Drake on many policies, he believes he is better qualified to “prosecute the case against the Republicans.”
“I’ve studied political science in college, I’ve studied the way that Alabama politics work. I understand the Republican philosophy,” he said. 
If elected, House said his first priority in office would be to pass a constitutional amendment prohibiting the drawing of legislative districts for partisan gain.
In April, the U.S. Supreme Court substantially weakened Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act in a case known as Louisiana v. Callais, raising the bar for racial discrimination in legislative districts but allowing partisan redistricting. Texas, California, South Carolina, Tennessee, Florida and Virginia have either redistricted to give either party more guaranteed congressional seats in the 2026 midterm elections, or are in the process of doing so. 
House said he also wants to establish a $15-per-hour minimum wage in the state. According to a study by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a livable wage for an adult with no children is $21.06 per hour. He said he also wants to pass “fair tax policies.”
“The federal government should raise the national minimum wage, but we can’t just wait on them to act. If they don’t, then our state representatives and senators need to pass legislation to raise the state minimum wage to a living wage,” House said. 
The general election
In November, voters will choose between the Democratic nominee and Roberts, who was the only Republican candidate to qualify for the race. The 34-year-old ran for Congress in 2022 in a race that U.S. Rep. Dale Strong would win, and got 13.8% of votes in the primary, according to election results. 
In an April interview, Roberts said he would prioritize workforce development, improving infrastructure and economic development. He said in a phone interview Friday afternoon that he is also concerned about affordability.
“I guess just overall, just affordability and cost of living right now, we certainly feel it when we go to the grocery store and at the gas pump,” he said. “We’re tuned into those things, but there’s only a certain amount that the state can do.”
Campaign fundraising
As of the most recent campaign filings, Roberts raised over $252,000 and has spent more than $34,000; Drake raised about $4,100 and spent about $1,000; and House has not reported any fundraising but has spent $3,000 of his own money.
How to vote
District 2 voters can choose between Drake or House for the Democratic nomination on June 16. The deadline to register to vote in the primary is Monday. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Polling locations can be found here. The winner will face Roberts in the general election on Nov. 3.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Overpaying for the status quo in West Virginia’s primary election
description: Five. Million. Dollars. In less than ten weeks. Mostly from just ten groups. For one midterm legislative cycle primary. Not Senate seats. Not Congress. Not a general election. Not for the governor’s mansion. A closed primary for the West Virginia House of Delegates and West Virginia Senate. A remarkable investment for what is, on paper, […]
text:
The Lincoln Walks at Midnight Statue sits in front of the West Virginia state Capitol building in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lexi Browning/West Virginia Watch)Five. Million. Dollars. In less than ten weeks. Mostly from just ten groups. For one midterm legislative cycle primary. Not Senate seats. Not Congress. Not a general election. Not for the governor’s mansion. A closed primary for the West Virginia House of Delegates and West Virginia Senate. A remarkable investment for what is, on paper, a minor ideological adjustment to the West Virginia Republican supermajority.
Millions of dollars were spent on more advertisements than there were outlets to run them on or hours in the day to watch them. Mailboxes overflowing with campaign mailers that ranged from the mundane to vicious manipulations. Months of an electorate subjected to unsolicited visual, audio and postal assault with demands to care about the 2026 primary election. The latest most important election there ever was against the dark forces of those who will do that to you if you don’t vote. 
Only 21% of voters showed up to do so. A shockingly poor return on investment in time and treasure from a political ecosystem that has never thought itself more important and never been better funded. Five million dollars, big name organizations, big name politicians involved, every possible advertising angle used and only 21% bothered to react at all. 
That does not compute. 
Five-million-dollar primaries and six–figure legislative grudge matches ought to buy more engagement. It’s easy to blame the politicians that have a supermajority that isn’t super enough for them; it’s even easier to blame big money outsiders and medium money insiders. The easiest is to blame the minority of voters who elected those politicians, while judging the majority who didn’t participate at all. The politically aggrieved that did not get their way will blame “the system,” “the voters” or “the money.”
Normally, something that costs $5 million but only has a 21% conversion rate would demand an audit of what is going wrong. But the truth is nothing went wrong. All the incentives for all the participants created the political money cycle the state of West Virginia finds itself in.
The money people sell the politicians on the ability to buy engagement with the voters. The voters prove election after election that logic is suspect at best. Yet the politicians keep leaning on the money people rather than trying to witness and understand the voters, making the next cycle worse. For the politicians’ part, they are both captured by the money loop and complicit in it. If they don’t spend money, someone else will spend it against them. Paying the consultant class and leaning on the donor infrastructure also means taking a shortcut past dealing with voters directly. 
The problem arises because while overlapping in function, the donor/consulting class and the office holders themselves have misaligned objectives. The politicians very much have to win for advancement or pay in career backsliding for losing. For the donor machine and consultant class, winning and losing is secondary to keeping those running paying for the services they provide. The candidates themselves are interchangeable, as long as they toe the line and vote “the right way” once in office.
A supermajority that starts to eat itself on petty points of purity has a large dose of feeding the money machine “the big bad” that brings the donations. With a supermajority that mostly agrees, the manufactured emergency of having the “right kind of” fill-in-the-blank nomenclature will have to do. And all those organizations funneling the money to candidates are just fine with the big bad being internal, manufactured or otherwise. The politician eats the loss; the money folks just move on to the next one. 
All the while, the voters themselves are mostly opting out of the whole exercise. The perpetual campaign era has learned to need voters less as voters have learned the same about it. Low voter turnout isn’t voter apathy so much as voters making the only determination years of lived experience tell them about their role in self-governing: it doesn’t matter very much. 
In the 2026 West Virginia primary the political operatives were on full send: In money spent, in mailers spamming mailboxes, in political ads on every available platform every available minute of every day. All of it focused on getting voters to care about very specific policy goals and organizational strategies from groups they’ve mostly never heard of involving people most of them had never met. 
Of course, all factions spending money, time and resources will say this was all for the voters, all for West Virginia, all for the betterment of everyone. The return on investment of that message and all that money was 21% turnout to weigh in on this, the latest most important election of their lifetimes. About 21% of registered West Virginia voters who turned out are not the result of the 2026 midterm election, they are the metric to measure what the rest of the voting population is or is not doing. West Virginians who didn’t need $5 million in spending to do what they always do on Election Day. 
The result of this primary election was that 79% of registered West Virginian voters subjected to millions of dollars in mailers and campaign ads demanding they care didn’t feel like finding the new polling location since the old school closed, nor driving on deteriorating roads to vote on a Tuesday.
To them, it wasn’t worth it.

name: Michigan Advance
title: If common ground exists in Lansing, it wasn’t on display at Mackinac’s legislative panel
description: MACKINAC ISLAND – Like the rest of the state, the politically divided Michigan Legislature is having trouble finding common ground, and the perpetual drama between the two chambers was on full display during this year’s Mackinac Policy Conference. Each year, the conference hosts a panel discussion with the respective leaders of the state House of […]
text:
Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, left, and House Speaker Matt Hall, right, speak during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)MACKINAC ISLAND – Like the rest of the state, the politically divided Michigan Legislature is having trouble finding common ground, and the perpetual drama between the two chambers was on full display during this year’s Mackinac Policy Conference.
Each year, the conference hosts a panel discussion with the respective leaders of the state House of Representatives and Senate. The panel gives attendees and observers from around the state a glimpse into how the two chambers are working together — or against each other — to solve the state’s biggest challenges.
The conference’s theme this year was “a quest for common ground,” a questionable premise with the state and its residents appearing more divided than ever, and the perception by many that business leaders didn’t have the pulse on working people’s problems.
Several attendees throughout the week told Michigan Advance that they, too, were skeptical that the conference’s conception of common ground might be a relic of the past. They also remained skeptical that the conference had the ability to make lasting change for middle- to lower-income earners.
On Thursday, the final event was a panel featuring Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids), House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt (R-Porter Township) and House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton).
Michigan Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, House Speaker Matt Hall, Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt and House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri speak during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
If the panel was meant to further the conference’s quest for common ground, it failed to do so, as simmering tensions finally boiled over.
The biggest hurdle the Legislature will face this year, as in many years, is the upcoming fiscal year budget. The statutory deadline to complete negotiations is July 1, a self-imposed target to enable the state’s public schools to know how much money they’ll receive from the state as they start their fiscal years. There are no consequences for the Legislature if they miss that deadline, other than scrutiny from schools and their stakeholders. 
The real deadline is Oct. 1, the date prescribed by the Michigan Constitution to have a budget deal completed and signed by the governor’s office.
Last year, the 2025-26 fiscal year budget came together only after the Legislature blew that final deadline and after an hour-long government shutdown. With the 2026 election season on the horizon, House and Senate observers were hopeful that the need to leave Lansing sooner than later might motivate the chambers to get a budget deal on time.
The panel discussion, however, revealed that the leaders do not see eye-to-eye on how quickly they could hammer out a new budget. It was also revealed that they hadn’t done much negotiating during their time on Mackinac Island.
“We have a lot of work to do, but we can do it if folks are committed to getting in a room and making decisions that need to be made in negotiating the details,” Brinks told panel host Zoe Clark of Michigan Public. “My goal remains to get it to the governor’s desk on time for her to review it and have it signed by July 1.”
That gives the Legislature just one month to hammer out the details. Does that give them enough time to get it done?
“Oh, we’ll see,” Hall said in response. “We had a great meeting, leader Brinks and I and the governor before we came down here. We started some of the table setting, which was good. But I told the leader, and I’ll say it here, once they drop the tax increases and the efforts to raid the rainy day fund, we’ll probably get a deal pretty quickly.”
Those preconditions set by Hall could prove to be this year’s sticking point.
Competing visions for Michigan’s future
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has proposed a set of tax increases to make up for lower than expected revenue projections and the loss of one-time federal funding left over from the COVID years. The Senate and the governor also see eye-to-eye on using rainy day funds to help bolster this year’s budget. Hall and his Republican colleagues have said that was a non-starter, as they want to eliminate property taxes. The GOP House believes it can continue to cut the budget and backfill those cuts with new revenue from luxury service taxes.
Those factors do not bode well for a consensus budget to form any time soon. Hall in particular is hanging his hat on the property tax reforms, which the governor’s office has indicated it has no interest in signing into law.
Nesbitt said that families are getting squeezed by the state’s budgeting processes, and that it is becoming harder for families to make ends meet. Nesbitt, a candidate for governor this year, didn’t mention the fact that national pressures, such as the imposition of tariffs and foreign policy decisions being made by the administration of President Donald Trump, were having some of the biggest impacts on people’s wallets.
The Senate’s minority leader said he hoped they could return to Lansing and pass some of the House Republican bills that the Senate likely has no interest in taking up, and not the budget overall.
Puri, who could be in line to become the House speaker if Democrats retake the chamber next year, turned the attention back to the budget and the need to get it done on time.
“It’s no different than last year,” Puri said. “Lansing Democrats were screaming from the rooftops on the importance of getting it done on time. The reality is that we have a sizable budget here in Michigan, which millions of Michiganders count on for critical programs that help them across the state.”
Puri added that it was unfortunate when leadership in his chamber, pointing to Hall, has “a warped sense of reality, and wants to continue to use every opportunity to turn everything into a political football, the people of Michigan suffer.”
Michigan Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt and House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri speak during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Bare-knuckle boxing at the Grand Hotel
This is when the gloves started to come off, and all sense of forging common ground ended for the discussion.
Hall accused Puri of having a “negative governing philosophy.” The speaker also invoked another area of tension between the two House caucuses: the participation of former House Speaker Joe Tate (D-Detroit). Tate had become sidelined after the House under his watch failed to push key Democratic priorities over the finish line in a chaotic 2024 lame duck session. He reemerged after Hall named him the House Appropriations Committee minority vice chair, which undoubtedly will drive a wedge between Democrats and their GOP colleagues.
“The difference is Joe Tate will work with us to get a deal, and will represent your caucus well,” Hall said with a grin. “We want to ensure that there’s a vibrant Democrat party with real leaders. … And we’ll do that. We’ll bring in Joe Tate and we’ll get a deal. And he’ll actually participate, something you didn’t do in the last budget.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That led to questions about who is actually at the negotiating table: The triumvirate of Whitmer, Brinks and Hall? Or Joe Tate and other legislative actors? When Clark asked the panel exactly who was doing the negotiating, the panel sat silent for several seconds.
Brinks finally broke the silence, saying that, from her perspective, it was state Sen. Sarah Anthony (D-Lansing), the Senate’s appropriations chair. She also threw some figurative sand back in Hall’s face.
“She’s very good at it, and that might be what he’s concerned about,” Brinks said of Anthony and Hall. “We are going to continue to do what we’ve done in the past. There’s been a proven procedure of how to get a responsible, balanced budget done, on time, for the people of Michigan.”
Brinks said that wasn’t new, and that Republicans used to know how to get such a budget done on time. That has changed with Hall in office as speaker, she said. Later in the discussion, Brinks accused Hall’s budget proposal as blowing a $5 billion hole in next year’s funding by eliminating much without making it revenue neutral.
Hall said he envisions the negotiations coming down to him and Whitmer and Brinks, but he was still advocating for pushing out Puri, bringing in Tate and involving Nesbitt somehow. That plan effectively also shuts out the House’s appropriations chair, state Rep. Ann Bollin (R-Brighton Township).
At one point in the discussion, Brinks also laid into Hall, noting his penchant for pontification, which she said would set him up nicely “for your next job.” 
“I will also add that listening to the folks here, it’s very difficult to take you seriously when you devolve into insults rather than focusing on the task at hand,” Brinks told Hall. “Or when you call everything waste, fraud or pork, when these are essential services that the people of our state rely on and they have paid for. The COVID dollars that came to us were meant to ease the pain and suffering of the people of Michigan and they were expended to do so.”
Brinks also called on Hall and Nesbitt to stop relitigating past budget fights and other woes. 
“Four of the last eight years, Republicans were in control,” Brinks said. “So it would be really helpful if you could avoid personal insults and start arguing your policies and your budget ideas on the merits of those ideas. Keep it simple and just get it done.”
Michigan Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt speaks during the Mackinac Policy Conference on Mackinac Island, Mich., on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
Will the election help or hurt the budget process?
Clark brought up the specter of the upcoming election, and how Brinks’ and Hall’s members need them to get it together so they can get back into their districts and campaign for their reelection efforts.
Hall said his focus was not on getting out to go and campaign, but rather to engage with Whitmer and Brinks and keep them at the table to solve Michigan’s various problems. The chamber highlighted those problems at the outset of the event, noting Michigan’s education and economy being ranked near last. Hall added legislative accountability to that mix.
“If we can stay in a little longer and solve that problem, that would be a meaningful change for the people of Michigan,” Hall said.
Nesbitt also said Michigan was at a crossroads.
“We can either just tinker around with the status quo over the next few years, and we’re going to continue to be in the bottom 10 in education, job growth, job opportunities, income growth and education,” Nesbitt said. “Or we can actually shake up the status quo in Lansing. Whether it’s lowering costs … these are real things for real people.” 
Despite the back and forth, no one in the room seemed to acknowledge that Flint was still suffering from its 2010-era water crisis, nor that both parties voted nearly unanimously to create a state economic development plan in 2021 that produced few results despite warnings from some lawmakers that it wouldn’t create the kinds of jobs its proponents were hoping for.
Those who went to Mackinac Island last week in search of common ground instead witnessed infighting and panel discussions with half-hearted solutions, leaving one to ask whether the annual meeting was anything more than an opportunity for lawmakers to get their last public jabs in before the real hard work toward finalizing a budget begins.

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

A Detroit-based law firm announced a class action lawsuit against a company operating a data center in Dowagiac, arguing that the noise the facility emits during its 24/7 operations has kept nearby residents from using and enjoying their property, Michigan Advance reported on Wednesday.
Yet another Michigan community is weighing a moratorium on data centers, MLive Local Government Reporter Melissa Frick wrote. On June 8, the Allendale Township Board of Trustees is set to vote on a measure that would block development of data centers, battery storage facilities and large-scale solar farms and wind farms for a year.

News of Note

Over the long Memorial Day weekend, a group of protestors speaking out against the University of Michigan and Los Alamos National Laboratory’s planned supercomputing facility drew police attention, according to MLive Washtenaw County Reporter Jennifer Eberbach. Following a late night demonstration outside University Vice President of Government Relations Chris Kolb’s home, six individuals were identified and cited for disorderly conduct.  Ann Arbor Police has since determined that the citations were issued improperly, and they will be void, Eberbach reports.
A recent poll released by The Glengariff Group coinciding with the kickoff of the Mackinac Policy Conference showed a majority of Michigan residents would oppose the construction of a data center within 25 miles of their home, with broad support for regulations on facilities looking to set up shop in their community. Michigan Advance Senior Reporter Ben Solis broke down the results, alongside voters’ answers about jobs and inflation.
As part of Bridge Michigan’s election year survey, the majority of Michigan’s candidates for governor shared their thoughts on data centers within the state, with Capitol Reporter Simon D. Schuster noting all candidates agreed new data centers should not increase electricity rates for residents.
Among the discussions at the Mackinac Policy Conference, former U.S. Secretary of Energy and 47th governor of Michigan Jennifer Granholm; Google’s head of data center market development and policy, Liz Schwab; and John Rakolta III, president of the building design and construction company Walbridge sat for a panel moderated by MichAuto Executive Director Glenn Stevens Jr. focusing on data centers as a community asset. While panelists said these facilities could bring several benefits to Michigan communities including clean energy resources, grid upgrades, tax revenue, Michigan Advance spoke with environmental advocates who said communities need more certainty and protections if they plan to host a data center.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island is burning through cash to build housing. It’s hardly made a difference, RIPEC says.
description: Record levels of funding and continued efforts by state leaders to cut red tape have barely made a dent in solving Rhode Island’s housing crisis, according to a new report from the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC). The 35-page analysis of the state’s housing landscape released last week by the business-backed research group analyzes […]
text:
A home under construction in Providence's Silver Lake neighborhood. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Record levels of funding and continued efforts by state leaders to cut red tape have barely made a dent in solving Rhode Island’s housing crisis, according to a new report from the Rhode Island Public Expenditure Council (RIPEC).
The 35-page analysis of the state’s housing landscape released last week by the business-backed research group analyzes the return on investment from the $120 million housing bond voters approved in 2024. 
“The vast majority of recent funding has been directed toward newly constructed units for a relatively small number of households, producing no meaningful impact on housing affordability for the large majority of residents,” the report states.
As of April 2026, $52.2 million from the bond had financed 200 newly constructed rental units at an average development cost of $512,377 per unit, with the state subsidizing roughly 51% of those costs.
Based on spending from the 2024 housing bond and projections tied to a similar proposal this year, RIPEC estimates the state’s investment will produce 642 new housing units statewide — enough to meet just 28.5% of the production goal set in the Executive Office of Housing’s 2030 plan.
RIPEC’s analysis projects it would take nearly $6 billion in state funding to bridge Rhode Island’s housing gap of 23,222 affordable rental units.
“This is an inefficient and unsustainable path that requires a strategic shift to ensure a real return for taxpayers and an increase in housing production,” RIPEC President and CEO Michael DiBiase said in a statement. “We should not continue to ask taxpayers to fund a model that fails to benefit the vast majority of Rhode Islanders.”
That model is one of high costs and high subsidies that prioritizes projects requiring capital grants, permanent operating vouchers, and ongoing service funding. Another contributor to high construction costs are the state’s varying environmental mandates typically absent in private-market builds, RIPEC noted
“Subsidized projects are frequently used as vehicles for non-housing policy objectives, including green building certifications, labor requirements, and community benefit agreements,” the report states. “While these mandates serve broader public interests, they significantly inflate the hard costs of construction.”
RIPEC recommends the General Assembly place strict requirements on future housing bonds, with at least half of any funds being dedicated to middle-income housing rather than deeply subsidized projects.
Emily Marshall, spokesperson for the Executive Office of Housing, disputed claims that the state is at risk of missing its 2030 targets. In a statement to Rhode Island Current, she noted nearly 3,800 housing permits were issued across each of Rhode Island’s municipalities in the last year — above the 3,000 per year goal set in the plan adopted by the state last December.
“While formal tracking toward Housing 2030 begins this year, that level of production reflects strong momentum driven by our investments and policy direction,” Marshall said. “Rhode Island’s housing strategy reflects a coordinated, fiscally responsible approach to increasing supply, preserving affordability, and modernizing housing delivery.”
A key feature of that approach is “the disciplined use of public resources to address gaps the private market does not fill,” she added. 
“These projects are revitalizing underutilized sites, strengthening local tax bases, and catalyzing neighborhood investment, while also supporting construction jobs and related economic activity across the state,” Marshall said. “By pairing housing production with infrastructure improvements and long-term affordability requirements, these investments are helping stabilize communities and improve quality of life for residents.”
But House Minority Leader Mike Chippendale, a Foster Republican, said in his own statement that permits don’t equal homes.
“For the past five years, the General Assembly has pushed a policy of more spending, more mandates, more centralized control, and less local authority,” he said in a statement.
Chippendale has long been critical of how much the state has spent in subsidizing new construction projects. Last fall, he called for a formal audit of RIHousing for perceived bloat and inefficiency at the quasi-governmental agency that finances affordable home construction.
RIPEC’s report also singles out RIHousing, mainly for its overlapping functions with the State Executive Office of Housing, which create a fragmented institutional landscape “where lines of authority are often unclear.”
“While the Executive Office of Housing now leads the policy agenda and sets the state’s strategic vision, RIHousing maintains departments that mirror these functions,” the report states. “These redundancies, potentially slow the delivery of units even as the state increases its fiscal commitment.”
RIPEC recommends lawmakers clarify the statutory roles between the two entities and consolidate its production programs to prevent excessive red tape.
RIHousing was still reviewing the RIPEC report as of late Friday but a spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the report “oversimplifies some of the challenges associated with housing development and affordability.”
Amy Rainone, director of government relations and policy, said comparing affordable housing construction and redevelopment projects to building conventional market-rate duplexes is hardly an apples-to-apples assessment of costs, scope, or outcomes.
“Many of our developments involve the rehabilitation of long-vacant or distressed properties, environmental remediation, required infrastructure improvements, long-term affordability requirements, or housing for populations whose needs are not typically met through the private market alone,” Rainone said. “Those projects will significantly vary from the costs associated with private-market new construction of two- and three-unit buildings.”
Rainone added that the relationship between RIHousing and the Executive Office of Housing has evolved since the office was reorganized and rebranded in 2025 by the General Assembly but both have distinct roles.
“Rhode Island’s housing challenges developed over decades and require coordinated efforts across the public, private, and nonprofit sectors,” Rainone said. “RIHousing remains committed to working with our partners to expand housing opportunities, leverage public resources effectively, support developments that strengthen communities across the state, and work together to bring Rhode Islanders home.”

title: Applicants sought to replace Leggett, Werner on Blueprint board
description: The body that oversees the state's multibillion-dollar education reform plan is accepting applications until Friday for candidates to fill two board seats set to come open July 1,.
text:
From left, Blueprint for Maryland's Future Accountability and Implementation Board Vice Chair William "Brit" Kirwan, Chair Isiah "Ike" Leggett and state Board of Education President Joshua Michael at a joint meeting of the boards last week. Leggett's term on the board is up July 1. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The body that oversees the state’s multibillion-dollar education reform plan is seeking applications for two seats set to come open July 1.
Applications will be accepted until 5 p.m. Friday from people who want to join the seven-member Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board, also known as the AIB.
An AIB nomination committee will review the applications for the seats currently held by AIB Chair Isiah “Ike” Leggett and Robin Werner, and recommend replacements to Gov. Wes Moore.
Leggett, the former Montgomery County executive, has served and chaired the board since it first met in November 2021. Werner, who works as director of teaching and learning for public schools in Talbot County, was appointed in August to replace Mara Doss, a former associate vice president for teaching, learning and student success at Prince George’s Community College who attended her last meeting in June 2025.
State boards approve additional metrics to improve student achievement

All applicants are expected to have knowledge in areas such as postsecondary education policy, teaching in public schools and “strategies used by top-performing state and national education systems in the world.”
Part of the application includes a 500-word essay in response to this question: “What will you contribute to the success of the Accountability and Implementation Board?”
Applicants must also check “yes” or “no” to several other questions such as delinquencies on federal, state, or local taxes or other debt; complaints of discrimination; and “are you now under any violation of law excluding minor traffic offenses?”
The committee must submit at least two names for each seat to Gov. Wes Moore (D), who has 30 days after receiving the list to name the new board members, who will serve six-year terms.
The governor can reappoint Leggett and Werner, should they apply for reappointment.
The committee is slated to announce candidates whose names will be forwarded to the governor in July.
The Blueprint board, which held a joint meeting Thursday with the state Board of Education, is scheduled to convene again on June 18.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: As Beshear blasts politics at UK, he continues to appoint big donors to UK board
description: FRANKFORT, Ky. – In April Gov. Andy Beshear delivered a strong warning about partisan donors exerting “undue outside influence” on the direction of the University of Kentucky. Yet, a different kind of partisan donor – insiders – officially oversee Kentucky’s flagship state university. They are the governors’ appointees to the UK Board of Trustees, and […]
text:
A sign on the University of Kentucky's campus signals an ongoing board meeting in April 2026. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)FRANKFORT, Ky. – In April Gov. Andy Beshear delivered a strong warning about partisan donors exerting “undue outside influence” on the direction of the University of Kentucky.
Yet, a different kind of partisan donor – insiders – officially oversee Kentucky’s flagship state university.
They are the governors’ appointees to the UK Board of Trustees, and the amounts that UK trustees have given to advance the political career of Democrat Beshear have been both consistent and consistently generous.
The 16 people Beshear has appointed to the board – including their companies and members of their immediate families – have made 321 donations totaling $1,666,637 to Beshear’s political causes since his 2015 campaign for attorney general, according to an analysis by the Kentucky Lantern. That number continues to grow as most trustees now regularly give to a super PAC (In This Together PAC, Inc.) promoting Beshear’s exploration of a run for president in 2028.
That’s more money than the Kentucky Education Association, or Churchill Downs and its executives, or even London Mayor Randall Weddle and his family and business associates have donated to Beshear political causes over the same period.
Moreover, eight of those trustees have also hosted fundraising events for Beshear, according to records of the Kentucky Registry of Election Finance. 
And the total could be higher because since his reelection in 2023 Beshear has also been raising money for a second political committee to help his ongoing presidential ambitions (Heckbent Inc.) that does not disclose the names of its donors.
Gov. Andy Beshear speaks during and interview with MS NOW’s Ali Vitali. (Photo provided by MS NOW)
Biggest donors, curious timing
The top donor among the trustees is Jim Gray, the former Lexington mayor who served as Beshear’s Transportation secretary until he took on a new role as special advisor to the governor in April. Gray has given $296,000 to Beshear political committees since 2014, according to Kentucky Lantern’s analysis.
But seven other trustees (Chairman Britt Brockman, Todd Case, Alex Bone, Robert Vance, Ron Geoghegan, Skip Berry and honorary trustee Frank Shoop) also rank among Beshear’s very biggest donors – giving time and time again over the years and rolling up totals in the six figures.
Because state law requires the board to reflect the political party breakdown of the state, Democrat Beshear must appoint many Republicans to the board. And the newer Republicans are among Beshear’s most enthusiastic recent donors.
Consider: Elizabeth McCoy, a banker from Hopkinsville, who for well over a decade has been a political donor to mostly Republicans, including to Gov. Matt Bevin, who appointed her to the UK Board of Trustees in 2017. She served until 2022. 
But in the last week of April 2023, McCoy and her husband gave what online government databases of campaign contributions show was by far the largest political donation they ever made – contributions totaling $50,000 to help Beshear’s reelection.
The contributions were: $2,000 to the Beshear campaign, $30,000 to the Kentucky Democratic Party; and $18,000 to the Democratic Governors Association.
About two weeks later, Beshear appointed McCoy to the UK board.
Also in late August of 2023, online databases show that Janie Greer, executive vice president and director of the First National Bank of Manchester, and her parents combined to give $46,300 to help Beshear. ($40,000 to the Kentucky Democratic Party and $6,300 to the Beshear campaign.)
One month later, Beshear appointed Greer to the UK Board.
‘No one has been appointed because of any donation’
Beshear declined to be interviewed for this story. But Scottie Ellis, communications director for the Governor’s Office, replied to questions sent to her by Kentucky Lantern with this statement:
“Every appointment to the University of Kentucky Board of Trustees was confirmed by the Republican supermajority in the Senate. All contributions are legal, transparent and publicly reported, and no one has been appointed because of any donation. The appointees reflect regional and political diversity, and each is fully qualified and brings important experience to the board.”
UK board chair Britt Brockman (University of Kentucky photo)
Chairman Brockman has donated $175,500 to Beshear’s political causes including the donations of his immediate family members, Lantern’s analysis shows.
Brockman also declined to be interviewed, but released this statement: “I believe in Kentucky. I support people, candidates and causes I believe will advance this state. It is that simple and that is my motivation. My support of both Steve and Andy Beshear over more than a decade is an example of that. I believe that is also what motivates my colleagues on the board as well. They deeply believe in this state and want a brighter future for it. I don’t believe political contributions qualify people for appointments, nor should they disqualify them.”
For their parts, most of the trustees who donated large amounts – including McCoy and Greer – did not return phone messages from Kentucky Lantern. The Lantern did reach Shoop, Geoghegan and Lucas.
Lucas referred questions to the UK administration. Geoghegan and Shoop said they donate to Beshear because they are longtime friends and supporters of him. They said they were not trying to enhance their chances for appointment to the UK board.
Senate President Robert Stivers, a Manchester Republican, could address the issue of Senate confirmation of Beshear appointees. But Stivers declined comment for this story. House Speaker David Osborne, of Prospect, was among the Republican officials who  criticized Beshear’s recent comments as unnecessarily disruptive. But Osborne also declined to comment.
The current clash
Beshear touched off the current conflict in April with a social media post saying he was losing confidence in UK’s leadership, citing two particular actions – the creation of an ill-defined job for retiring Athletics Director Mitch Barnhart that paid $1 million a year, and the appointment of U.S. District Judge Gregory Van Tatenhove as dean of the law school without full approval of the school’s faculty.
Beshear said he was worried that these decisions “are related to certain donors pushing partisan and undue influence on the university.”
Since then, Barnhart has stepped away from the new job, but President Eli Capilouto has stood firm behind Van Tatenhove’s appointment, saying that under governance changes made in 2024 the board of trustees no longer must approve the appointment of the law school dean.
At a board meeting later in April Gray won board approval for a group of university stakeholders to be appointed to review and revise governing regulations to allow for a board “vote on these kinds of appointments going forward.”
Beshear said later at a press conference, “I’m going to take a real close look at the board of trustees to make sure we’re getting real strong oversight, and they should absolutely walk back what’s claimed to be the 2024 action that moved these decisions to the president.”
‘A disturbing pattern’
Ross Mugler, chief executive of the Washington-based Association of Governing Boards of Universities and Colleges, said trustee appointments to any state’s flagship university “are highly coveted, very sought-after.”
And Mugler says the reason goes beyond the luxury box trappings that trustees enjoy at basketball and football games.  
Mugler said, “Trustee service at a flagship is widely viewed as both a significant civic responsibility and a prestigious leadership opportunity.”
And just as there is an age-old practice of presidents appointing big donors to ambassadorships, Mugler said it has long been common for governors in Kentucky and other states to appoint big donors to university boards.
But Mugler said his experience has been that these big donors have been dedicated board members.
“Most of them bring excellent leadership skills to the boardroom,” Mugler said. “I think you’ll find that 90 percent of them are doing it for the right reason.”
Some Kentucky Republicans, however, believe Beshear’s appointments of big donors have gone too far, raising the question of whether contributions are the most important qualification.
Tres Watson, a Republican political consultant from Lexington, said, “There has been – for years – a disturbing pattern in the connection between donations to Beshear political committees and his appointments to the UK board, as well as his appointments in general.”
Former Kentucky Senate Majority Leader Damon Thayer, a Georgetown Republican, said that because so many big donors have gotten appointments, “I’m convinced Andy Beshear is the most transactional governor we’ve had in 50 years.
“It’s all kind of a dirty little secret in Frankfort,” Thayer said. “For Andy Beshear to talk about the exercise of undue partisan influence – outside or inside – is pretty rich.”
The law on appointments
State law gives the governor authority to directly appoint 13 of the 20 members of the University of Kentucky Board of Trustees. The governor also appoints three alumni members, but for each of these he must pick one of the top three vote-getters in an election conducted by the alumni association.
The faculty elects two members of the board, the staff employees elect one, and the student body president serves on the board.
Currently there is one honorary trustee, longtime trustee Frank Shoop. As an honorary trustee, Shoop can participate at meetings and enjoys all perks and privileges of a trustee. But he cannot vote at meetings.
The governor’s appointments are subject to confirmation by the Kentucky State Senate. 
State law also requires that the governor’s appointees to “reflect proportional representation of the two leading political parties based on the state’s voter registration.” 
There are currently eight Democrats and eight Republicans among Beshear’s appointed trustees. That does not include Shoop or the student, faculty and staff appointees.
The law also requires that the governor’s appointees “no less than proportional representation of the minority racial composition of the Commonwealth based on the total minority racial population.”
The Lantern’s analysis showed alumni trustees have given just $1,050 to Beshear causes. The current faculty, staff and student donors have not contributed.
Many ways to give to Beshear
Beshear has raised so much money from appointees – and apparently so much more than previous governors – largely because he has been raising money for a long time and for much more than just his three successful campaigns for statewide office.
He began fundraising in 2013 while his father Steve Beshear was governor with a goal of winning election in 2015 for attorney general. He built up an early war chest (on contributions limited at that time by state law to $1,000 per person) that scared off serious opposition in the Democratic primary of 2015 and won the general election by a razor-thin margin.
Then came his win in the 2019 primary for governor. After that, Beshear became the leader of the Kentucky Democratic Party which has raised money to help Beshear through his narrow win in the 2019 governor’s race and a more comfortable reelection in 2023.
Well-heeled donors, corporations and labor unions have also had legal avenues to give contributions of unlimited amounts to Beshear: to the Democratic Governors Association, to super PACs running independent campaigns for Beshear’s elections, to committees that paid for his inaugural ceremonies.
A month after his 2023 reelection Beshear formed the two committees – In This Together and Heckbent – which have been raising money ever since.
Nine of the current UK trustees have consistently donated to Beshear for the entire journey – starting with donations to the attorney general’s race through recent contributions to In This Together.
Comparison to Bevin 
Republican Matt Bevin got little or no contributions from 11 of the 12 persons he named to the UK Board. Kentucky Lantern found those 11 combined to give less than $30,000 to Bevin’s two campaigns for governor and to the Republican Party of Kentucky between May of 2015 and December of 2019.
The one exception was a huge one – Kelly Craft, appointed by Bevin as a UK trustee in August of 2016.
Kelly and Joe Craft at a reception in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 26, 2017 after she became U.S. ambassador to Canada. (Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images for Kelly Craft)
Craft is the wife of billionaire coal magnate and longtime UK benefactor Joe Craft, who appears to be the target of Beshear’s concerns about outside donors having out-sized influence at UK. 
Their financial support for Bevin’s gubernatorial campaigns was extensive and included hosting a big fundraiser in 2015 after Bevin won an upset victory in the Republican primary for governor and hosting two more fundraisers for Bevin in 2019, Kentucky Registry of Election Finance records show. Executives and employees of Craft’s Alliance Coal showered bundles of small contributions totaling $100,000 to Bevin’s two campaigns. Joe Craft and entities he heads (including Alliance Coal and JWC III Revocable Trust) gave more than $700,000 to the Republican Governors Association in the two years Bevin ran for Kentucky governor.
Kelly Craft served as a UK trustee for about 14 months, resigning after President Trump appointed her as U.S. ambassador to Canada.
But any comparison of Beshear and Bevin contributions comes with some caveats. First, Beshear has been raising money for a much longer period of time (for three statewide campaigns compared to two for Bevin) and for many more political committees that support his political career. Second, Bevin was in office making appointments for four years, while Beshear has been governor for six and a half years. Finally, Bevin self-funded a significant portion of his two campaigns for governor. 



About Kentucky Lantern’s analysis:
Sources: Federal Election Commission website, Kentucky Registry of Election website, Internal Revenue Service website for contributions to political organizations. ProPublica’s online “527 Explorer” was invaluable in helping the search for contributions to political organizations that report to the IRS.
Process: The list of contributions represents the best effort by Kentucky Lantern to search the sources listed above for contributions by Beshear’s appointees to the University of Kentucky Board of Trustees (and their identifiable immediate relatives and companies) to political committees that have advanced Andy Beshear’s political career. Those committee’s are: Beshear’s 2015 campaign for attorney general; Beshear’s 2019 campaign for governor; Beshear’s campaign for governor in 2023; the Kentucky Democratic Party since May of 2019; Beshear’s super PAC In This Together; the Democratic Governors Association in 2015 and in 2023 to present; super PACs that backed Beshear’s 2019 and 2023 campaigns for governor (Bluegrass Values, Defending Bluegrass Values, and Kentucky Family Values); Beshear’s inauguration committees in 2109 and 2023; Democratic Grassroots Victory Fund in 2023; and a small PAC that backed Beshear in 2019 called Bluegrass Committee for Progress.
